ocar.opportunity: How a wiring diagram constrains the activity a nervous system can produce is still an open question. The complete C. elegans connectome makes it possible to test whether structure alone can generate recognizable behavior-like patterns.
ocar.challenge: Most circuit models either ignore the rest of the worm or bake in detailed cell physiology. It is unclear whether a feeding circuit studied in isolation behaves like the same neurons sitting inside the full network.
ocar.action: George, Puppo, and Silva (bioRxiv, 2020) simulated dynamics on the known worm connectome using a model in which local interactions among connected cells generate global activity without molecular detail. They stimulated the chemosensory neuron ASEL in a feeding circuit both alone and embedded in the full wiring map, then tracked time-ordered signal walks they call Temporal Sequences (TSeq).
ocar.resolution: Contralateral ventral (VB) and dorsal (DB) motor-neuron activations emerged that were qualitatively similar to rhythmic firing linked to crawling. Only 5% of TSeq from the isolated feeding network were preserved when that network was embedded; 95% of isolated signaling paths were absent from the full connectome.
ocar.future_work: The authors treat this as a caution that isolated-circuit simulations can mislead. A natural next step is to test other behaviors and stimuli with the same isolated-versus-embedded comparison.

summaries.beginner: Scientists asked whether the worm’s known wiring map can, by itself, produce activity that looks like crawling. Stimulating one taste cell in a feeding circuit did yield walking-like motor patterns, but almost all of the signal routes seen in the small circuit vanished once the same cells sat inside the whole worm network.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv in 2020, George, Puppo, and Silva asked how C. elegans structural connectivity constrains dynamics, using a model in which local interactions generate global activity without biophysical cell detail. Stimulating ASEL in a feeding circuit, both isolated and embedded in the full White-style connectome, produced contralateral VB/DB motor activations reminiscent of locomotion. Their Temporal Sequence (TSeq) analysis found that only 5% of signaling walks survived embedding; 95% of isolated-network paths were absent from the full graph.
summaries.advanced: The dynamics are qualitative and independent of molecular cell detail, so they cannot claim biophysical realism. The 5%/95% TSeq split is a strong warning about isolated-circuit modeling, but it is specific to ASEL stimulation of one feeding circuit and to this particular dynamical formalism. The ‘purposeful wiring’ interpretation is proposed, not experimentally proven.

plain_language_summary: Scientists asked whether the worm’s known wiring map can, by itself, produce activity that looks like crawling. Stimulating one taste cell in a feeding circuit did yield walking-like motor patterns, but almost all of the signal routes seen in the small circuit vanished once the same cells sat inside the whole worm network.

ocar.opportunity: A dense adult Drosophila central-brain connectome makes it possible to treat a real brain as a complete directed graph, within experimental error, rather than a sampled sketch.
ocar.challenge: It is not obvious which graph statistics matter for function, or how a biological wiring diagram compares with human-designed logic systems.
ocar.action: Scheffer (bioRxiv, 2020) treated the fly central-brain connectome as a directed graph with weighted edges and surveyed input/output distributions, wiring randomness, compartment differences, path lengths, proximity of strong connections, known computational motifs, electrical response versus compartment structure, and packing efficiency.
ocar.resolution: The preprint frames these measurements as a way to speculate on function by comparing biological graph properties with engineered logic. It emphasizes that density—all nodes and links represented within experimental error—is what makes the comparison meaningful.
ocar.future_work: The abstract is a survey prospectus rather than a single headline result; follow-up would be to tie specific graph features to identified computations in named compartments.

summaries.beginner: Once almost every connection in the adult fruit-fly central brain was mapped, researchers could treat that map like a complete directed network. This paper lists the network features worth measuring and asks how they might shape what the fly brain can do.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, Louis K. Scheffer analyzes the dense adult Drosophila central-brain connectome as a directed, weighted graph. Because the map aims to include all nodes and links within experimental error, he compares biological wiring with human-designed logic systems across degree distributions, compartment differences, path lengths, strong-connection proximity, known computational structures, and packing. The goal is to speculate how those graph properties could affect function.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not report numerical findings, so claims about function remain speculative. ‘Dense within experimental error’ still admits missed or false synapses. Comparisons with engineered logic systems are analogies, not proofs of computational role.

plain_language_summary: Once almost every connection in the adult fruit-fly central brain was mapped, researchers could treat that map like a complete directed network. This paper lists the network features worth measuring and asks how they might shape what the fly brain can do.

ocar.opportunity: The developing C. elegans connectome is a rare setting in which every neuron’s birth time and eventual wiring can be related. Standard network statistics already show a rich club inside a small-world graph, pointing to integrative computation.
ocar.challenge: Those statistics miss weakly connected motifs such as topological cavities that might support segregated computation, and it is unclear how robust growing topology is to noisy birth times.
ocar.action: Helm, Blevins, and Bassett (bioRxiv, 2020) used persistent homology to track cavities in the growing worm connectome through development, tested robustness to birth-time perturbation, compared with growth models, and asked whether a neuron’s birth-time consequence tracks other biological properties.
ocar.resolution: Developing topology was relatively robust to birth-time changes and was not captured by similar growth models. Growing topology was nonetheless especially sensitive to the exact birth times of a small set of mostly motor neurons, and appeared distinct from other network properties.
ocar.future_work: The authors anticipate that these measurements will help build more accurate models of C. elegans neuronal development.

summaries.beginner: As a tiny worm’s nervous system grows, the pattern of connections changes in ways that ordinary network scores can miss. Tracking those hidden ‘holes’ in the wiring over time showed a stable growth pattern that still depends on when a few motor cells are born.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv in 2020, Helm, Blevins, and Bassett applied persistent homology to the growing C. elegans connectome to follow topological cavities through neural development. Unlike rich-club and small-world statistics, this approach can detect weakly connected motifs potentially relevant to segregated computation. Growing topology was relatively robust to neuron birth-time changes, was not reproduced by similar growth models, and was particularly sensitive to a small set of predominantly motor neurons.
summaries.advanced: Robustness is described as relative, not absolute, and ‘not captured by similar growth models’ depends on which models were compared (not enumerated in the abstract). Linking birth-time sensitivity to other biological properties is posed as a question. Persistent homology describes topology, not physiology.

plain_language_summary: As a tiny worm’s nervous system grows, the pattern of connections changes in ways that ordinary network scores can miss. Tracking those hidden ‘holes’ in the wiring over time showed a stable growth pattern that still depends on when a few motor cells are born.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans wiring map can be read as an information-processing network: about 90 sensory neurons, about 80 interneurons, and about 120 motor neurons. That architecture invites comparison with encoder–decoder networks that compress then expand signals.
ocar.challenge: Feedforward flow from sensors to muscles is tangled with recurrent and feedback paths, so it is hard to see whether information must pass through a small bottleneck.
ocar.action: Sabrin, Wei, van den Heuvel, and Dovrolis (PLoS Computational Biology, 2020) applied an ‘hourglass effect’ analysis to feedforward sensory-to-motor flow, checking robustness to how feedforward versus feedback is separated and to chemical synapses versus chemical synapses plus gap junctions.
ocar.resolution: Feedforward flow traversed a waist of 10–15 interneurons, largely the same cells previously identified as the worm’s rich club. The core set stayed mostly the same under alternative feedforward/feedback splits and synapse types. The authors interpret the waist as an information bottleneck balancing accuracy against compactness.
ocar.future_work: The encoder–decoder analogy suggests testing whether those core interneurons encode compressed sensory states that are reused combinatorially by motor output.

summaries.beginner: In the worm, many sense cells talk to many muscle-control cells through a middle layer of go-between cells. This study finds that messages are squeezed through a small set of those middle cells, like an hourglass waist.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2020), Sabrin and colleagues treated the C. elegans connectome as a processor with about 90 sensory, 80 inter-, and 120 motor neurons. Hourglass analysis of feedforward sensory-to-motor flow identified a waist of 10–15 interneurons that largely overlap the previously reported rich club. The result was robust to feedforward/feedback separation and to chemical synapses versus chemical synapses plus gap junctions, suggesting an information-bottleneck architecture akin to encoder–decoder networks.
summaries.advanced: Hourglass analysis concerns feedforward flow, not the highly recurrent interneuron graph in full. Overlap with the rich club is described as ‘mostly’ the same cells. The encoder–decoder analogy is interpretive. Neuron-class counts (~90/~80/~120) and waist size (10–15) should be treated as the paper’s reported ranges, not independent measurements.

plain_language_summary: In the worm, many sense cells talk to many muscle-control cells through a middle layer of go-between cells. This study finds that messages are squeezed through a small set of those middle cells, like an hourglass waist.

ocar.opportunity: Serotonin-releasing neurons ramify widely to modulate many behaviors, yet their wiring at single-cell resolution has been largely unknown. A whole-brain electron-microscopy volume of a female Drosophila now makes a complete partner list feasible.
ocar.challenge: A single identified serotonergic neuron (the CSDn) spans several olfactory regions with glomerulus-to-glomerulus differences, so it is unclear whether those differences reflect output specializations, input diversity, or both.
ocar.action: Coates and colleagues (Journal of Neuroscience, 2020) reconstructed CSDn connectivity across olfactory areas in the whole-brain EM dataset, comparing antennal-lobe versus lateral-horn patterns and hunting non-olfactory partners.
ocar.resolution: In the antennal lobe, glomerular innervation differences reflected diverse presynaptic partners rather than glomerulus-specific output, which was predominantly onto local interneurons, with subtype-specific relationships. Across regions, even individual projection neurons that span areas had different CSDn connectivity; the lateral horn showed more distributed, transmitter-biased contacts. Novel partners from other sensory domains provided strong top-down input.
ocar.future_work: The significance statement frames this wiring logic as a ground plan for heterogeneous modulatory effects; next experiments would test those predicted local versus extrinsic influences physiologically.

summaries.beginner: A single serotonin cell in the fruit fly reaches many smell-related brain areas, but until a whole-brain electron-microscope map existed, no one had listed all of its partners. The map shows that this cell listens and talks differently in each area, and that other senses can strongly drive it.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience (2020), Coates et al. used a female Drosophila whole-brain EM volume to map the CSDn, a broadly projecting serotonergic neuron spanning olfactory regions. Antennal-lobe glomerular differences were driven by diverse inputs, with output mainly to local interneurons in a subtype-specific way, whereas the lateral horn showed more distributed, transmitter-based targeting. Novel non-olfactory partners supplied strong top-down input, illustrating region-specific mixing of local and extrinsic synapses.
summaries.advanced: The reconstruction is one female brain; partner weights and polarity are EM-inferred, not functionally confirmed in this abstract. ‘Strong’ top-down input is qualitative. CSDn is one identified serotonergic neuron, not a survey of all serotonergic cells.

plain_language_summary: A single serotonin cell in the fruit fly reaches many smell-related brain areas, but until a whole-brain electron-microscope map existed, no one had listed all of its partners. The map shows that this cell listens and talks differently in each area, and that other senses can strongly drive it.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics needs huge amounts of labeled synapses and mitochondria, but expert time is scarce. Active learning can spend that time on the most useful unlabeled examples.
ocar.challenge: Typical query-suggestion models train only on the small labeled set, so they become less helpful on the harder unlabeled images that actually need annotation.
ocar.action: Lin et al. (ECCV, 2020) proposed two-stream active query suggestion: a supervised feature extractor plus an unsupervised extractor trained on all raw images, later fine-tuned with new labels. They built an end-to-end active-learning framework for 3D synapse detection and mitochondria segmentation.
ocar.resolution: They curated what they describe as the largest connectomics dataset with dense synapse and mitochondria annotation. On it, the method outperformed previous state-of-the-art by 3.1% (synapses) and 3.8% (mitochondria) in region-of-interest proposal accuracy, and also beat prior approaches on CIFAR-10 under the same limited annotation budget.
ocar.future_work: The two-stream idea is not limited to EM; the CIFAR-10 result suggests testing whether unsupervised features similarly help other biomedical labeling tasks with tiny budgets.

summaries.beginner: Teaching a computer to mark synapses and mitochondria in brain images usually needs many expert labels, which are expensive. This work asks the computer to choose the most useful unlabeled pictures to mark next, using both labeled and unlabeled images, and reports better detection with the same labeling budget.
summaries.intermediate: At ECCV 2020, Lin and colleagues introduced two-stream active query suggestion for connectomics: a supervised stream plus an unsupervised stream trained on all raw images so query selection does not collapse onto the small labeled set. They applied the idea to 3D synapse detection and mitochondria segmentation and released a large densely annotated dataset. Region-of-interest proposal accuracy improved by 3.1% for synapses and 3.8% for mitochondria over prior state of the art, with a matching win on CIFAR-10 under a limited annotation budget.
summaries.advanced: Gains are for ROI proposal accuracy, not full instance segmentation quality. ‘Largest’ is the authors’ claim. CIFAR-10 is a natural-image sanity check, not EM. Unsupervised features help only if raw-image diversity matches the unlabeled pool the annotator will see.

plain_language_summary: Teaching a computer to mark synapses and mitochondria in brain images usually needs many expert labels, which are expensive. This work asks the computer to choose the most useful unlabeled pictures to mark next, using both labeled and unlabeled images, and reports better detection with the same labeling budget.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila larva lets researchers combine synapse-resolution wiring maps with cell-resolution activity and behavior maps. That combination is a path to how brains implement general computations such as multisensory integration, learning, and action selection.
ocar.challenge: Even with maps in hand, it is not obvious where modalities first converge or how early sensorimotor loops differ from higher-order, valence-like signals.
ocar.action: Eschbach and Zlatic (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2020) review larval connectomics as a ‘road map,’ highlighting early versus centralized multisensory convergence.
ocar.resolution: They argue that early multisensory convergence recruits specific sensorimotor loops for specific actions, whereas higher-order brain areas integrate modalities more centrally and produce valence-like signals for goal-oriented behavior.
ocar.future_work: The review points toward using these maps to pin down neural implementations of integration, learning, and action selection in the larva.

summaries.beginner: The fruit-fly maggot is small enough that scientists can map its wiring, watch cells fire, and score behavior in the same animal. This review explains how those maps show simple sense-to-movement loops sitting beside higher brain areas that mix senses into like-versus-dislike signals.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2020), Eschbach and Zlatic review Drosophila larva as a system that combines comprehensive synapse-resolution connectivity with cellular activity and behavior maps. They propose that this approach can reveal implementations of multisensory integration, learning, and action selection. Early convergence is said to recruit specific sensorimotor loops, while higher-order areas integrate more centrally and emit valence-like signals for goal-directed behavior.
summaries.advanced: This is a highlights-style review, not a new reconstruction. Claims about early versus centralized integration are synthesis from the literature cited in the piece, not quantified here. Transfer to adult fly or vertebrates is not established in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: The fruit-fly maggot is small enough that scientists can map its wiring, watch cells fire, and score behavior in the same animal. This review explains how those maps show simple sense-to-movement loops sitting beside higher brain areas that mix senses into like-versus-dislike signals.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics usually reverse-engineers existing brains. Synthetic biology instead builds systems from parts; combining the two could yield live organisms whose wiring is designed rather than only observed.
ocar.challenge: There is no agreed picture of what a synthetic connectome would look like, what it would be for, or how it could be constructed.
ocar.action: Rabinowitch (Physics of Life Reviews, 2020) outlines synthetic connectomics as a program: artificially design and construct connectomes of living, behaving organisms, and sketches first implementation steps plus scientific and societal impact.
ocar.resolution: The review argues that building wiring would be a powerful test of theories of network function, a platform for studying brain operation, and possibly a route to new forms of artificial life.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a prospectus; the implied agenda is to move from conceptual design to constructible circuits in tractable animals.

summaries.beginner: Most brain-mapping work takes existing animals apart. This essay asks what we would learn if we instead designed and built a living nervous system’s wiring from the ground up.
summaries.intermediate: In Physics of Life Reviews (2020), I. Rabinowitch proposes synthetic connectomics: forward-engineering the connectomes of live behaving organisms as a counterpart to reverse-engineering maps. The review asks what a synthetic connectome would look like, what purposes it would serve, and how it could be built. Construction, the author argues, would be a stringent test of network-function theories and a possible path to new forms of artificial life.
summaries.advanced: No empirical construction is reported. Societal-impact claims are speculative. Feasibility depends on tools for specifying synapses in vivo that the abstract does not demonstrate.

plain_language_summary: Most brain-mapping work takes existing animals apart. This essay asks what we would learn if we instead designed and built a living nervous system’s wiring from the ground up.

ocar.opportunity: Animals reuse the same motor neurons for different actions. Drosophila larva forward versus backward crawling is a compact place to ask how one motor pool can produce opposite behaviors.
ocar.challenge: Without a complete premotor-to-motor wiring diagram for a segment, it is hard to know whether labeled lines, combinatorial wiring, morphology, or circuit motifs explain the switch.
ocar.action: Zarin, Mark, Cardona, Litwin-Kumar, and Doe (eLife, 2019) measured larval muscle recruitment, reconstructed with TEM a full segment of all 60 motor neurons and 236 premotor neurons, analyzed that connectome, built a recurrent network model, and tested selected predictions with optogenetics.
ocar.resolution: All body-wall motor neurons were active in both behaviors, but a subset changed recruitment timing. The connectome contained labeled-line connectivity, combinatorial PMN–MN links, asymmetric morphology, and motifs that could all contribute. The model reproduced the behaviors, and optogenetics validated selected predictions.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the premotor–motor connectome as a foundation for analyzing the larva’s full behavioral suite.

summaries.beginner: The same muscle-control cells in a maggot help it crawl both forward and backward. Mapping every local partner of those cells, then modeling and testing the circuit, showed that timing—not a wholly separate set of cells—helps switch direction.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2019), Zarin et al. combined larval muscle recordings with TEM reconstruction of an entire segment (60 motor neurons and 236 premotor neurons) to explain forward versus backward locomotion. All body-wall motor neurons participated in both behaviors; a subset changed recruitment timing. Connectome analysis found labeled-line and combinatorial premotor–motor wiring, asymmetric morphology, and motifs; a recurrent model reproduced the behaviors, with optogenetic tests of selected predictions.
summaries.advanced: Reconstruction is one segment, not the whole larva. Model-to-behavior match and ‘selected’ optogenetic tests do not exhaust alternative motifs. Dual-behavior activation of all body-wall MNs is a strong constraint on labeled-line-only theories.

plain_language_summary: The same muscle-control cells in a maggot help it crawl both forward and backward. Mapping every local partner of those cells, then modeling and testing the circuit, showed that timing—not a wholly separate set of cells—helps switch direction.

ocar.opportunity: Faster electron microscopes now produce volumes too large for manual cell instance segmentation, in neuroscience and in cell biology. Networks already help, but accuracy still lags humans.
ocar.challenge: Segmentation networks have a limited field of view, so they cannot use expected cell shape or other biological priors that people rely on, leaving heavy proofreading.
ocar.action: Pape et al. (Frontiers in Computational Science, 2019) encoded domain knowledge as long-range interactions in a lifted multicut graph-partitioning problem.
ocar.resolution: On three challenging EM segmentation problems from neuroscience and cell biology, the lifted-multicut formulation significantly improved accuracy relative to not using those long-range biological constraints.
ocar.future_work: The same idea—casting morphology priors as long-range lifted edges—could be applied to other EM tissues where local networks still fail on large cells.

summaries.beginner: Computers that outline cells in electron-microscope pictures often miss the big picture of cell shape that a person would use. This paper lets those shape rules act like long-distance hints in a puzzle, and reports clearer cell outlines on several hard datasets.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Computational Science (2019), Pape and colleagues argue that convolutional segmenters’ limited field of view blocks use of morphological priors. They express domain knowledge as long-range interactions in a lifted multicut partitioning problem. The formulation yielded significant accuracy gains on three challenging EM instance-segmentation tasks spanning neuroscience and cell biology.
summaries.advanced: ‘Significant improvement’ is not given as a numeric delta in the abstract. Lifted constraints help only if the prior is correct; wrong morphology rules could propagate. The method still sits on top of automatic proposals, so local CNN errors remain a bottleneck.

plain_language_summary: Computers that outline cells in electron-microscope pictures often miss the big picture of cell shape that a person would use. This paper lets those shape rules act like long-distance hints in a puzzle, and reports clearer cell outlines on several hard datasets.

ocar.opportunity: To watch how a whole animal turns wiring into movement, models need the nervous system, muscles, and body in one place, with pieces that can be swapped as data improve. C. elegans has a complete connectome that can anchor such a stack.
ocar.challenge: Existing simulations rarely let users exchange intracellular, synaptic, muscle, or mechanical modules, or systematically ablate cells to hunt unknown sensorimotor paths.
ocar.action: Kim, Santos, Alkema, and Shlizerman (bioRxiv, 2019) built modWorm, a modular C. elegans neuro-mechanical framework with seven exchangeable modules from intracellular dynamics through proprioceptive feedback, then stimulated known locomotion neurons, applied external body forces, and ran in-silico ablations.
ocar.resolution: The base model recapitulated forward and backward locomotion and mid-run avoidance/turns when known stimuli were applied. Ablation surveys inferred novel circuits. Swapping empirically based intra- and extra-cellular dynamics, plus parameter optimization, was used to compare simulated locomotion with experiments.
ocar.future_work: The framework is offered as a way to keep identifying circuits that control, mediate, and generate natural behavior as modules improve.

summaries.beginner: To see how a worm’s wiring produces crawling, researchers built a computer worm whose nerve, muscle, and body pieces can be swapped. Poking known cells in the model made it crawl, reverse, and turn, and silencing cells pointed to extra circuits to test.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2019), Kim et al. introduced modWorm, a modular C. elegans model integrating seven stages from intracellular dynamics and electrical/chemical synapses through muscle force, posture, and proprioception on the complete connectome. In-silico current injection into known locomotion neurons and external body forces recapitulated forward/backward crawling and avoidance turns; ablation surveys suggested novel sensorimotor circuits. Module variants were compared with experimental locomotion.
summaries.advanced: Recapitulation is in silico against known experimental associations, not a closed-loop fit to new kinematics in the abstract. ‘Novel circuits’ are model inferences. Constant-current injection and the chosen muscle/body modules will bias which paths appear sufficient.

plain_language_summary: To see how a worm’s wiring produces crawling, researchers built a computer worm whose nerve, muscle, and body pieces can be swapped. Poking known cells in the model made it crawl, reverse, and turn, and silencing cells pointed to extra circuits to test.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans pharynx is a small, self-contained neuromuscular organ with 20 neurons in 14 types—an anatomical entry point to feeding. A modern serial-EM pass can revise how that mini-nervous system is classified.
ocar.challenge: Earlier maps split pharyngeal cells into interneurons versus motor neurons and understated cross-connectivity, which may hide a shallow sensory-motor architecture.
ocar.action: Cook et al. (bioRxiv, 2019; Journal of Comparative Neurology venue listed on the record) re-reconstructed the pharyngeal connectome by serial EM and reclassified cells by likely sensory and motor roles, then compared neighbor association and synapse rates with the somatic nervous system.
ocar.resolution: Most pharyngeal neurons are likely also sensory, and most if not all also motor, with more extensive cross-connectivity than previously realized—a shallow network organized into modules matching known pharyngeal functional domains. Pharyngeal neurons physically associate with, and synapse onto, a larger fraction of neighbors than somatic neurons.
ocar.future_work: The authors speculate that this architecture may resemble ancestral primitive nervous systems, inviting evolutionary comparisons.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s throat has its own tiny nervous system of twenty cells. A new electron-microscope rebuild suggests most of those cells both sense and drive muscle, wired in a shallow web that matches the parts of the throat that do different jobs.
summaries.intermediate: Cook, Crouse, Yemini, Hall, Emmons, and Hobert (2019) used serial EM to re-evaluate the C. elegans pharyngeal connectome (20 neurons, 14 types). Contrary to a clean interneuron/motor split, most cells likely combine sensory and motor roles, with more cross-connectivity than previously mapped, forming modules aligned with known functional domains. Relative to the somatic nervous system, pharyngeal neurons contact and synapse with a larger fraction of neighbors.
summaries.advanced: Sensory/motor labels are predictions from anatomy, not direct physiology in the abstract. Comparison with somatic statistics depends on equivalent synapse-calling criteria. The ancestral-nervous-system speculation is explicitly framed as speculation.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s throat has its own tiny nervous system of twenty cells. A new electron-microscope rebuild suggests most of those cells both sense and drive muscle, wired in a shallow web that matches the parts of the throat that do different jobs.

ocar.opportunity: Head-direction representations are widespread, and theory says they may live in ring attractors with specific excitatory and inhibitory motifs. Drosophila’s heading circuit is small enough to test those wiring assumptions directly.
ocar.challenge: The assumed E/I connectivity has been hard to measure, so models could not be confirmed or rejected at synapse resolution.
ocar.action: Turner-Evans et al. (bioRxiv, 2019) reconstructed the fly heading circuit with EM, added RNA profiling of identified types, then used genetically targeted two-photon imaging and thermogenetic perturbations during behavior.
ocar.resolution: They found motifs hypothesized to hold heading in darkness, update it during turns, and tether it to visual cues, with physiology supporting those roles. They also found unanticipated recurrence between mixed pre/post arbors. The circuit contains core ring-attractor ingredients yet extra structure that may let few neurons track heading accurately.
ocar.future_work: The EM-plus-RNA dataset is offered as a reference for future functional studies of the network.

summaries.beginner: Many animals keep an internal sense of which way they are facing. In the fruit fly, a detailed wiring-and-activity study shows a ring-like circuit that can hold, update, and visually lock that heading—plus extra loops that simple models had not included.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2019), Turner-Evans and colleagues combined EM circuit reconstruction and RNA profiling of Drosophila heading-direction cell types with two-photon imaging and thermogenetic perturbation. They identified motifs matching ring-attractor proposals for maintaining heading in darkness, updating it on turns, and tethering it to visual cues, and they report supporting physiology. Unexpected mixed pre/post recurrence was also present, suggesting extra structure for accurate tracking with few neurons.
summaries.advanced: Motifs ‘consistent with’ models are not a unique proof of attractor dynamics. RNA profiling and EM come from identified types but not necessarily the same cells as the physiology. Mixed-arbor recurrence remains functionally underexplained in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Many animals keep an internal sense of which way they are facing. In the fruit fly, a detailed wiring-and-activity study shows a ring-like circuit that can hold, update, and visually lock that heading—plus extra loops that simple models had not included.

ocar.opportunity: Female flies avoid geosmin, a mold odor, when laying eggs—an innate, ethologically grounded behavior. Tracing that aversion from sensors to descending output would show how valence is wired.
ocar.challenge: Innate odor responses could be a labeled line all the way down or a distributed central code; without a complete synaptic path, those alternatives stay verbal.
ocar.action: Huoviala et al. (2018 preprint) identified second-, third-, and fourth-order neurons required for geosmin egg-laying aversion and placed them on a connectomics path from sensory input to descending neurons.
ocar.resolution: They found multilevel valence-specific convergence, including axo-axonic input onto second-order neurons that carry another danger cue (parasitoid wasp pheromone), but also massive divergence: second-order geosmin neurons contact about 80 third-order types, where aversive channels converge. Descending neurons critical for the aversion sit one layer further. The data suggest a shift from peripheral labeled lines to a distributed central representation coupled to distinct descending paths.
ocar.future_work: The implied program is to test how that distributed third-order layer selects among descending routes during real egg laying.

summaries.beginner: Female fruit flies avoid a mold smell when they lay eggs. Researchers traced the cells needed for that avoidance from the nose-like sensors down to output cells that drive action, finding both dedicated danger lines and a wide mix in the central brain.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2018 preprint, Huoviala, Dolan, Jefferis and colleagues identified second- through fourth-order neurons required for Drosophila geosmin egg-laying aversion and placed them on a sensory-to-descending connectome. They report valence-specific convergence, including axo-axonic contacts onto wasp-pheromone second-order neurons, plus divergence onto about 80 third-order types where aversive odors converge. Descending neurons critical for the behavior sit one layer further, consistent with a labeled-line periphery feeding a distributed central code.
summaries.advanced: ‘Required for’ is causal at the neurons tested, but completeness of the path depends on the connectome used. The count of ~80 third-order types is anatomical diversity, not proof each type is behaviorally necessary. Journal field is empty on this record; treat as preprint.

plain_language_summary: Female fruit flies avoid a mold smell when they lay eggs. Researchers traced the cells needed for that avoidance from the nose-like sensors down to output cells that drive action, finding both dedicated danger lines and a wide mix in the central brain.

ocar.opportunity: Neuron segmentation is advancing, but a wiring diagram also needs synaptic partners. Insect synapses are especially hard because one presynaptic site contacts multiple postsynaptic partners.
ocar.challenge: Standard pipelines expect expensive voxel labels of clefts or vesicles rather than the point annotations people actually collect.
ocar.action: Buhmann et al. (MICCAI, 2018) trained a 3D U-Net to classify long-range edges between voxels as directed synaptic pairs, learning from synaptic point annotations.
ocar.resolution: On the MICCAI 2016 CREMI challenge they improved over the then state of the art, producing 3% fewer errors than the next-best method.
ocar.future_work: Direct pair prediction from points should transfer to other polyadic insect volumes where cleft painting is the bottleneck.

summaries.beginner: In insect brains, one sending site often talks to several receiving partners, which makes automatic synapse listing hard. This method learns those sender–receiver pairs from simple point marks instead of fully painted synapses and made fewer mistakes on a public contest set.
summaries.intermediate: At MICCAI 2018, Buhmann, Funke and colleagues formulated Drosophila-style synaptic partner detection as classification of long-range voxel edges encoding pair presence and direction. A 3D U-Net learned those pairs from point annotations rather than cleft or vesicle masks. On the 2016 CREMI challenge they reported 3% fewer errors than the next-best method.
summaries.advanced: The 3% is versus the then CREMI leader, not a full connectome error rate. Point annotations still assume partners are marked; missed polyadic partners remain possible. Generalization beyond CREMI is not quantified here.

plain_language_summary: In insect brains, one sending site often talks to several receiving partners, which makes automatic synapse listing hard. This method learns those sender–receiver pairs from simple point marks instead of fully painted synapses and made fewer mistakes on a public contest set.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans connectome has been known for decades, yet locomotion control is still under-constrained because synapse signs (excitation versus inhibition) are mostly missing. Even a seven-neuron pre-motor circuit has a combinatorially huge sign pattern.
ocar.challenge: Brute-force enumeration of excitation/inhibition assignments is intractable, and signs must be consistent with both neurophysiology and behavior.
ocar.action: Rakowski and Karbowski (PLoS Computational Biology, 2017) combined genetic algorithms, large-scale parallel search, and detailed interneuron modeling, scoring patterns against locomotory data.
ocar.resolution: The best-matching pattern made all interneuron connections inhibitory, including those onto motor neurons. That matches emerging cholinergic-signaling data and suggests an energy-saving design.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue the result grounds more realistic neural-control models and that the search method can be applied, possibly modified, to other small C. elegans circuits.

summaries.beginner: Knowing who talks to whom in a worm does not say whether each talk is a push or a pull. Searching many possible push/pull patterns for a small walking circuit found a best fit in which the middle cells mostly inhibit, a design that may save energy.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2017), Rakowski and Karbowski inferred synaptic polarities in a seven-neuron C. elegans pre-motor locomotion circuit. They coupled genetic algorithms and parallel search to neurophysiological models scored on behavioral data. The optimal match was all-inhibitory interneuron connections, including onto motor neurons, consistent with then-recent cholinergic signaling results and interpreted as metabolic thrift.
summaries.advanced: Optimality is relative to the model, cost, and behavioral data used; other sign patterns could score close. ‘All inhibitory’ is for this seven-cell circuit, not the whole worm. Energy-saving is an interpretation of the sign pattern, not a calorimetry result.

plain_language_summary: Knowing who talks to whom in a worm does not say whether each talk is a push or a pull. Searching many possible push/pull patterns for a small walking circuit found a best fit in which the middle cells mostly inhibit, a design that may save energy.

ocar.opportunity: Automated reconstruction from serial-section EM hinges on neuronal boundary detection. 2D max-pooling convnets were the standard on highly anisotropic volumes.
ocar.challenge: Anisotropy (weaker quality along z) limits naive 3D nets, while shallow 2D nets underuse depth and 3D context.
ocar.action: Lee, Zlateski, Vishwanathan, and Seung (NeurIPS, 2015) trained a much deeper hybrid 2D–3D recursive architecture: a first net’s preliminary boundary map, plus the image, feeds a second net. Training used ZNN, a multicore-CPU 3D convnet implementation.
ocar.resolution: The three changes—depth, mixed 2D/3D filters, and recursion—yielded a substantial accuracy gain on anisotropic EM boundary detection. The authors suggest the hybrid design may apply to other anisotropic 3D data, including video, and recursion to labeling problems generally.
ocar.future_work: Extending the recursive 2D–3D stack beyond boundary detection to full neuron labeling is the obvious next use.

summaries.beginner: Brain electron-microscope stacks are sharp in the plane of each slice but blurrier between slices, which makes drawing cell borders hard for computers. A deeper network that looks both in-plane and across slices, then refines its own first guess, drew better borders.
summaries.intermediate: At NeurIPS 2015, Lee, Zlateski, Vishwanathan, and Seung improved anisotropic serial-section EM boundary detection with a deeper hybrid 2D–3D convolutional net and recursive training: a second network sees the image plus a first-pass boundary map. ZNN accelerated 3D backprop on multicore CPUs. They report a substantial accuracy gain over the 2D max-pooling standard.
summaries.advanced: ‘Substantial gain’ is not given as a numeric score in the abstract. Recursive training can amplify first-pass errors. ZNN targets CPU parallelism; later GPU U-Nets changed the engineering baseline. Applicability to video is suggested, not shown.

plain_language_summary: Brain electron-microscope stacks are sharp in the plane of each slice but blurrier between slices, which makes drawing cell borders hard for computers. A deeper network that looks both in-plane and across slices, then refines its own first guess, drew better borders.

ocar.opportunity: Mouse mesoscale tract-tracing can weight, distance, and cost whole-brain projections, letting topology and wiring cost be compared in one directed connectome.
ocar.challenge: Wiring-cost minimization explains many features of embedded brains but not all; integrative hubs may be expensive for a reason.
ocar.action: Rubinov, Ypma, Watson, and Bullmore (PNAS, 2015) analyzed 461 anterograde-tracer injections into right cortical and subcortical mouse regions, performing multiscale topological and spatial analysis and comparing participation with independent histology and gene expression.
ocar.resolution: The mouse connectome was small-world and hierarchically modular, with greater-than-minimal wiring costs. High-participation hubs mediated between localized modules, were especially costly, matched default-mode-like regions, and colocalized with low neuronal density and cognition-related gene expression. The authors propose competing pressures: cost minimization versus hub-mediated integration.
ocar.future_work: The competitive-selection account predicts that perturbing expensive hubs should hit ‘higher-order’ functions harder than local modules—a test for later causal work.

summaries.beginner: Mouse brain maps show that some regions act as expensive crossroads linking specialized neighborhoods. Those crossroads are not what you would build if you only wanted the shortest wires; they look more like a compromise between saving wire and sharing information.
summaries.intermediate: In PNAS (2015), Rubinov et al. estimated weights, distances, and wiring costs from 461 anterograde-tracer injections in the right mouse hemisphere. The directed connectome was small-world and hierarchically modular with greater-than-minimal cost. High-participation hubs linked anatomically localized modules, aligned with default-mode-like regions, and matched low neuronal density plus cognition/learning-related gene expression—evidence for simultaneous cost and integration pressures.
summaries.advanced: This is mesoscale tracing, not synapse-level EM. Injections are right-hemisphere. Hub–gene associations are colocalization, not causation. ‘Greater-than-minimal wiring costs’ depends on the null model of spatial embedding.

plain_language_summary: Mouse brain maps show that some regions act as expensive crossroads linking specialized neighborhoods. Those crossroads are not what you would build if you only wanted the shortest wires; they look more like a compromise between saving wire and sharing information.

ocar.opportunity: Supervised multilayer nets already labeled images well, but residual errors still block practical connectomic reconstruction from 3D EM.
ocar.challenge: The authors hypothesized that existing nets were too narrow, too local, too feedforward in label space, and too slow to train.
ocar.action: Huang and Jain (ICLR, 2013) proposed DAWMR networks: thousands of features, large fields of view, recursive label-space iterations, a parallelizable architecture, plus a boundary-specific example-weighting scheme, released with open-source software.
ocar.resolution: On connectomic 3D EM, DAWMR reached new labeling performance. The top architecture had twelve layers, interwoven supervised and unsupervised stages, and a 54³ (157,464-voxel) field of view per prediction.
ocar.future_work: The software is meant to make such wide recursive stacks easy to assemble for other labeling tasks.

summaries.beginner: Computers labeling cell borders in 3D brain images still made enough mistakes to slow reconstruction. A wider, deeper network that looks at a large neighborhood and then revisits its labels improved those drawings.
summaries.intermediate: At ICLR 2013, Huang and Jain introduced Deep And Wide Multiscale Recursive (DAWMR) networks for image labeling, targeting connectomic 3D EM boundary prediction. The design uses thousands of features, a large field of view, recursive exploitation of label-space dependencies, and faster parallel training, plus a novel example-weighting scheme for boundaries. The best reported net had twelve layers with mixed supervised/unsupervised stages and a 54³-voxel context.
summaries.advanced: ‘New levels of performance’ is not accompanied by a numeric benchmark in the abstract. A 54³ FOV is computationally heavy. Recursive label iterations can entrench correlated errors. Later U-Nets changed the baseline this result should be judged against.

plain_language_summary: Computers labeling cell borders in 3D brain images still made enough mistakes to slow reconstruction. A wider, deeper network that looks at a large neighborhood and then revisits its labels improved those drawings.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding vertebrate vision needs a complete network graph of at least one retina. Better EM control, dataset software, and storage made synaptic connectomics practical.
ocar.challenge: Complete retinal graphs require high resolution, cell-identity tags, open volumes, and annotation tools; without them, reconstruction stays incomplete.
ocar.action: Marc, Jones, Lauritzen, Watt, and Anderson (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2012) review an optimal strategy: transmission EM at 2 nm or better, molecular tags, open-access volumes, and open-source annotation to build 3D cell libraries, network diagrams, and connectivity databases.
ocar.resolution: Early retinal connectomics already showed that even nominally well-studied cells have richer connection graphs than expected.
ocar.future_work: The implied goal remains a complete representative retinal connectome using that stack of methods.

summaries.beginner: To understand seeing, it helps to have a complete wiring list for a retina. This review describes how electron-microscope maps of mouse retina were becoming practical, and notes that familiar cell types already look more richly connected than textbooks suggested.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2012), Marc and colleagues argue that vertebrate vision needs a complete synaptic graph of a representative retina. They advocate TEM at 2 nm or better, molecular identity tags, open volumes, and open-source annotation. First retinal connectomics efforts showed richer-than-expected graphs even for well-studied cells, in the mouse-retina datasets associated with this record.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods-and-progress review, not a full connectome release. The 2 nm TEM criterion is a stated optimum, not a result. ‘Richer than expected’ is qualitative.

plain_language_summary: To understand seeing, it helps to have a complete wiring list for a retina. This review describes how electron-microscope maps of mouse retina were becoming practical, and notes that familiar cell types already look more richly connected than textbooks suggested.

ocar.opportunity: Large EM volumes for connectomes cannot be traced by hand. Neuron membrane detection is a required step toward automatic reconstruction.
ocar.challenge: Noise, anisotropic shape and brightness, and confounding structures make membranes hard to detect.
ocar.action: Jurrus et al. (Medical Image Analysis, 2010) applied a series of artificial neural networks on stencil-neighborhood intensity features, each network using the previous net’s classification as context.
ocar.resolution: Serial ANNs improved detection over traditional ANNs and over previous membrane methods, a step toward automated connectome reconstruction.
ocar.future_work: The serial-context idea is a precursor to later deep stacks; applying it inside full reconstruction pipelines is the stated direction.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope pictures of nerve tissue are noisy, so computers struggle to find cell membranes. Passing the image through a sequence of small neural nets, each seeing the last net’s guess, improved membrane finding.
summaries.intermediate: In Medical Image Analysis (2010), Jurrus and colleagues detected neuron membranes in EM using serial ANNs whose feature vectors are stencil-neighborhood intensities. Each network uses the prior network’s classification context. They report improved detection versus traditional ANNs and prior membrane methods, aiming at automated connectome reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: No numeric error rates appear in the abstract. Stencil ANNs are shallow by later standards. Serial context can propagate early mistakes. Anisotropy and confounders remain the core difficulty the method only partly absorbs.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope pictures of nerve tissue are noisy, so computers struggle to find cell membranes. Passing the image through a sequence of small neural nets, each seeing the last net’s guess, improved membrane finding.

ocar.opportunity: Nanoscale connectomics is too slow for whole mammalian brains. Expansion microscopy raises effective resolution, and X-ray tomography is a fast volumetric readout that might beat serial EM on throughput.
ocar.challenge: Expansion enlarges tissue volume cubically, increasing imaging time, and no group had yet shown cellular X-ray contrast inside expanded tissue.
ocar.action: Collins (2026) combined modified enzymatic Unclearing, a metallic gold stain, and laboratory X-ray microscopy to image expanded tissue.
ocar.resolution: The report is presented as the first reconstruction of cell bodies in expanded tissue with X-ray microscopy (expansion X-ray microscopy, ExXRM). Neurites were not resolved because of extensive off-target staining.
ocar.future_work: The author stresses that ExXRM must still resolve neurites, reduce off-target stain, and be adapted to faster synchrotron X-ray microscopy before it is useful for connectomics.

summaries.beginner: Mapping whole mammalian brains with electron microscopy is currently too slow. This early report shows that expanded tissue can be seen with X-rays well enough to pick out cell bodies, a first step toward a faster mapping method.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 report (no journal listed on this record), L. Collins addresses ExM’s cubic volume penalty and the lack of X-ray contrast in expanded tissue. Combining modified enzymatic Unclearing with gold stain and lab X-ray microscopy, the work claims the first X-ray reconstruction of cell bodies in expanded tissue. Neurites were not resolved due to off-target staining; synchrotron adaptation is flagged as required for speed.
summaries.advanced: This is explicitly an early-stage demonstration: cell bodies only, not synapses or neurites. ‘First’ is the author’s claim. Off-target gold staining is a current blocker. Laboratory X-ray throughput is far from synchrotron performance.

plain_language_summary: Mapping whole mammalian brains with electron microscopy is currently too slow. This early report shows that expanded tissue can be seen with X-rays well enough to pick out cell bodies, a first step toward a faster mapping method.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans is strikingly bilateral, so left–right neuron pairs might share network roles even when their individual synapses differ.
ocar.challenge: Bilateral pairs differ substantially in left–right connections; whether they still occupy similar network roles, and how, was unclear.
ocar.action: Kim, Song, Kralik, and Jeong (European Journal of Neuroscience, 2026) quantified bilateral redundancy in adult hermaphrodite and male connectomes with connectivity similarity, motif-fingerprint difference, and path compensation, plus null models that randomize asymmetric edges while holding symmetric ones.
ocar.resolution: Bilateral pairs showed elevated redundancy versus other pairs. Randomizing asymmetric edges reduced bilateral similarity, implying asymmetry itself helps pairs share neighbors and roles. In hermaphrodites, redundancy was stronger among interneurons than sensory neurons on all three measures; in males the gradient was significant only for path compensation.
ocar.future_work: The authors present bilateral redundancy as a multiscale principle that cannot be explained by symmetry alone, motivating developmental models that generate useful asymmetry.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s left and right nerve cells are not wired as perfect mirror images. This study finds that those imperfect pairs still play similar jobs in the network, and that the mismatches actually help them share partners.
summaries.intermediate: In European Journal of Neuroscience (2026), Kim et al. measured bilateral redundancy in adult hermaphrodite and male C. elegans connectomes using connectivity similarity, motif-fingerprint difference, and path compensation. Pairs were more redundant than other neurons. Null models that shuffled asymmetric edges while keeping symmetric ones reduced similarity, so asymmetry contributes to shared roles. Hermaphrodite interneurons were more redundant than sensory neurons on all three metrics; males showed that gradient only for path compensation.
summaries.advanced: Graph metrics are not physiology; shared roles are topological. Sex differences in which metric shows a sensory–interneuron gradient caution against pooling. Null-model conclusions depend on how ‘asymmetric edges’ are defined.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s left and right nerve cells are not wired as perfect mirror images. This study finds that those imperfect pairs still play similar jobs in the network, and that the mismatches actually help them share partners.

ocar.opportunity: Behaviors such as grooming require coordinated head, antenna, and foreleg motion. Drosophila antennal grooming is a tractable place to ask whether coordination is peripheral feedback or a centralized brain controller.
ocar.challenge: It is unknown whether each body part needs sensory feedback from the others, and which connectome neurons actually synchronize them.
ocar.action: Özdil et al. (Nature Communications, 2026) combined kinematics, a biomechanical model, perturbations (amputation/immobilization), an antennal-grooming network from the brain connectome, a simulated activation screen, and experimental manipulation of ‘asteroid’ broadcast inhibitory neurons.
ocar.resolution: Coordination enabled unobstructed, forceful tibia–antenna collisions in the biomechanical replay, and movements of one part did not require proprioception from the others. Connectome analysis pointed to centralized interneurons and shared premotor neurons. A simulated activation screen highlighted recurrent-excitation plus broadcast-inhibition motifs, and asteroid neuron manipulations supported the inhibition arm.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest similarly centralized controllers may be a general motif for co-recruiting body parts across behaviors.

summaries.beginner: When a fly grooms its antennae, head, antennae, and front legs move together. Experiments and a brain wiring map suggest a central controller coordinates them, rather than each part waiting on feedback from the others.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2026), Özdil, Ramdya and colleagues studied Drosophila antennal grooming. Biomechanical replay suggested coordination yields efficient tibia–antenna collisions. Amputation or head immobilization did not stop remaining parts from moving. A connectome-derived network implicated centralized interneurons and shared premotor cells; a simulated activation screen found recurrent excitation plus broadcast inhibition, with asteroid inhibitory neurons validated experimentally.
summaries.advanced: Lack of requirement for cross-part proprioception does not mean feedback is unused in intact animals. The activation screen is simulated. Generalization to locomotion is proposed, not shown. Unilateral versus bilateral grooming may load the same motifs differently.

plain_language_summary: When a fly grooms its antennae, head, antennae, and front legs move together. Experiments and a brain wiring map suggest a central controller coordinates them, rather than each part waiting on feedback from the others.

ocar.opportunity: Automated EM segmentation is essential at volume scale, but proofreading dominates cost. Knowing when the graph is ‘good enough’ would let projects stop rationally.
ocar.challenge: Estimating remaining proofreading needs usually requires ground truth that large datasets lack.
ocar.action: Martinez et al. (bioRxiv, 2026) tracked simple global graph invariants as edits accumulated, without a priori ground truth, on a zebrafish spinal cord and the Drosophila hemibrain.
ocar.resolution: Invariants converged predictably toward asymptotic limits with more edits, yielding a quantitative ‘pencils down’ criterion. The method is described as fast and computationally inexpensive and as reducing planning uncertainty for proofreading budgets.
ocar.future_work: Data owners could fit these curves early to budget remaining edits for a stated scientific question.

summaries.beginner: Fixing computer mistakes in huge brain maps is expensive, and it is hard to know when to stop. This paper shows that simple summaries of the connection graph settle toward a stable value as fixes accumulate, giving a practical stopping rule without a perfect answer key.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), Martinez and colleagues estimate connectomic proofreading progress from global graph invariants that converge toward asymptotes as edits accrue, without ground truth. They illustrate the approach on a zebrafish spinal cord and the Drosophila hemibrain. The curves are argued to provide a quantitative stopping criterion and a budget forecast for remaining edits.
summaries.advanced: Convergence of invariants is not the same as biological completeness; a stable wrong graph could still plateau. Results are shown on two datasets at different proofreading stages. Which invariant, and which scientific question, should set the threshold is a policy choice, not a unique optimum.

plain_language_summary: Fixing computer mistakes in huge brain maps is expensive, and it is hard to know when to stop. This paper shows that simple summaries of the connection graph settle toward a stable value as fixes accumulate, giving a practical stopping rule without a perfect answer key.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila flight is a classic model of visual information processing. Genetic access to single cell types plus a complete connectome now let circuit diagrams meet behavior from fast reflexes to longer goal-directed flight.
ocar.challenge: How visual signals become steering outputs, and how a small neuron set remains flexible enough for both stabilizing and goal-directed maneuvers, remains incompletely synthesized.
ocar.action: Schnell (Trends in Neurosciences, 2026) reviews recent findings on visually guided flight control in the fly.
ocar.resolution: The review argues that flexibility in visual processing and hierarchical recruitment of behavioral modules enable complex flight control with comparatively few neurons.
ocar.future_work: The implied research program is to map which modules are recruited under which visual and internal-state conditions using the connectome as a scaffold.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies steer in flight using vision, from quick corrections to longer goal-seeking. This review gathers new cell-type and wiring results to explain how a relatively small set of neurons stays flexible enough for both.
summaries.intermediate: In Trends in Neurosciences (2026), Bettina Schnell reviews how Drosophila transforms vision into flight output, spanning fast stabilizing responses and longer-lasting goal-directed behaviors. Genetic targeting, physiology, and the complete connectome are the enabling tools. The synthesis is that processing flexibility plus hierarchical module recruitment lets a comparatively small neuron set control complex flight.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; no new dataset is presented. ‘Comparatively small’ is relative to vertebrates, not a count. Hierarchical-module language is a framework, not a unique circuit proof.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies steer in flight using vision, from quick corrections to longer goal-seeking. This review gathers new cell-type and wiring results to explain how a relatively small set of neurons stays flexible enough for both.

ocar.opportunity: Single-neuron connectomes across species share small-world topology and heavy-tailed weights and degrees. If simple developmental geometry can generate those features, they may be universal rather than species-specific.
ocar.challenge: Distance-dependent wiring alone yields small-world graphs but not heavy-tailed distributions, so additional developmental rules are needed.
ocar.action: Morales-Gregorio, Kurth, and Korvasová (2026) analyzed connectomes from C. elegans, Platynereis, Drosophila, zebrafish, and mouse, then added weight-preferential attachment (synapse clustering along neurites) and degree-preferential attachment (arbor extent), exploring parameters systematically.
ocar.resolution: Distance dependence produced small-worldness; weight-preferential attachment added heavy-tailed weights; degree-preferential attachment added heavy-tailed degrees. Combined, the three rules reproduced characteristic empirical properties. The authors conclude activity-independent geometric constraints during development can account for conserved architecture across distant species.
ocar.future_work: The claim of universality invites tests against activity-dependent rules and against species whose geometry violates the fitted parameters.

summaries.beginner: Brain wiring in worms, flies, fish, and mice shares family traits such as mostly local links plus a few very strong or very busy cells. This study argues those traits can emerge from simple growth rules based on distance and on how branches and synapses cluster, without needing electrical activity.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 paper (no journal on this record), Morales-Gregorio et al. study single-neuron-resolution connectomes from C. elegans, Platynereis, Drosophila, zebrafish, and mouse. Distance-dependent connectivity produced small-world networks but not heavy tails; adding weight-preferential attachment (spatial synapse clustering) and degree-preferential attachment (arborization extent) recovered heavy-tailed weights and degrees together with small-world topology. They propose activity-independent geometric development as a conserved assembly mechanism.
summaries.advanced: Sufficiency of geometric rules is not exclusivity; activity-dependent mechanisms could yield the same statistics. Parameter exploration can overfit shared summaries. Mouse and fly volumes are partial relative to C. elegans completeness, which may affect tail estimates. ‘Activity-independent’ is a modeling assumption.

plain_language_summary: Brain wiring in worms, flies, fish, and mice shares family traits such as mostly local links plus a few very strong or very busy cells. This study argues those traits can emerge from simple growth rules based on distance and on how branches and synapses cluster, without needing electrical activity.

ocar.opportunity: MICrONS offers co-registered calcium imaging and EM reconstruction from the same mouse visual cortex, so cortical geometry, wiring, and function can initialize recurrent nets rather than remaining metaphors.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear which biological constraints actually help RNNs learn, and whether they induce brain-like organization.
ocar.action: Shakiba et al. (arXiv, 2026) used spatial coordinates, anatomical connectivity, and function-derived relationships from nearly 12,000 coregistered excitatory neurons to initialize recurrent weights and impose communication-aware spatial constraints on three cognitive decision-making tasks.
ocar.resolution: Structure-and-function-constrained nets outperformed baseline and partially constrained models. Functional weight initialization gave the largest gain; real spatial embedding added robust improvements. Networks developed low-entropy, modular, small-world organization and still performed well with excitatory-only recurrence.
ocar.future_work: The result motivates treating cortical inductive biases as first-class architecture choices for other tasks and inhibitory populations not included here.

summaries.beginner: A mouse visual-cortex dataset that pairs wiring with activity was used to start and constrain computer networks that have loops. Those biologically seeded networks learned decision tasks better than unconstrained ones and organized themselves in more brain-like ways.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2026), Shakiba, Dehghani and colleagues built RNNs from MICrONS data: coordinates, EM wiring, and function-derived relationships among nearly 12,000 coregistered excitatory neurons, plus communication-aware spatial constraints during learning. Across three cognitive decision-making tasks, fully constrained models beat baselines; functional initialization contributed the largest gain, spatial embedding further improvements. Learned nets were modular and small-world and remained strong even with positive-only recurrent weights.
summaries.advanced: Tasks are cognitive decision-making benchmarks, not the mouse’s visual behaviors. Only excitatory coregistered neurons are used. ‘Outperform’ magnitudes are not numeric in the abstract except the qualitative ranking. Positive-weight restriction is an ablation, not a Dale-law circuit.

plain_language_summary: A mouse visual-cortex dataset that pairs wiring with activity was used to start and constrain computer networks that have loops. Those biologically seeded networks learned decision tasks better than unconstrained ones and organized themselves in more brain-like ways.

ocar.opportunity: Multimodal, multiscale brain atlases are proliferating, but integrative analysis in one reference space remains hard from insects to primates.
ocar.challenge: Heterogeneous formats block comparison of gene expression, activity, light-level morphology, and EM synapses on the same cells.
ocar.action: Wang et al. (bioRxiv, 2026) present iBrAVE, an open-source platform that unifies datasets into five core representations for 3D interactive analysis, including morphology metrics, cross-modal spatial correspondence, and light–EM identity matching.
ocar.resolution: Single-modality tools include spatially resolved single-neuron morphology (geometry, topology, projection, clustering, putative wiring). Across modalities, gene expression and activity link to morphologically defined neurons. Across scales, bidirectional inference of identity and synaptic connectivity uses morphology matching between light and EM.
ocar.future_work: The authors position iBrAVE as a unified framework for data-driven discovery on future atlases.

summaries.beginner: Brain maps now come from genes, microscopes, and activity recordings, but they rarely sit in one place. iBrAVE is software that puts those maps into a shared 3D space so researchers can compare a cell’s shape, genes, activity, and connections.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), Wang, Du and colleagues introduce iBrAVE, an open-source platform for 3D integrative analysis of brain atlases across modalities and scales. Heterogeneous data are unified into five core representations, enabling source-independent analyses from insects to primates. Features include single-neuron morphology analytics, spatial linking of genes and activity to defined neurons, and bidirectional light–EM identity and synapse inference via morphology matching.
summaries.advanced: ‘Putative wiring’ and morphology-based EM matching are inferences, not guaranteed synapses. Five representations necessarily compress source-specific metadata. Cross-species claims depend on registration quality not detailed in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Brain maps now come from genes, microscopes, and activity recordings, but they rarely sit in one place. iBrAVE is software that puts those maps into a shared 3D space so researchers can compare a cell’s shape, genes, activity, and connections.

ocar.opportunity: Large EM volumes still yield oversegmented neuron fragments. Automatically proposing which fragments to merge would imitate human proofreading at scale.
ocar.challenge: Pixel-only segmenters miss global morphology; naively scoring all adjacent fragment pairs is intractable.
ocar.action: Chen, Chen, Wang, Xiong, and Wu (IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, 2026) built a connection-point detection network fusing global 3D morphology with high-resolution local image context via proposal-based sampling and cross-attention, then a connectivity-prediction network, forming a fully automatic merge pipeline.
ocar.resolution: Experiments supported the modules’ effectiveness and the pipeline’s robustness for large-scale neuron reconstruction. Code and data are released.
ocar.future_work: Released code invites testing on additional EM volumes where oversegmentation patterns differ.

summaries.beginner: Computers often chop a single nerve cell into many pieces in electron-microscope volumes. This method looks at both the overall 3D shape and the zoomed-in image at possible join points to decide which pieces belong together, copying how a person proofreads.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging (2026), Chen and colleagues address oversegmentation in EM neuron reconstruction with multimodal connection-point detection. The network fuses global 3D morphology with local image context via proposal-based feature sampling and cross-attention, then a second network predicts connectivity. The automatic merge pipeline is described as robust at large scale, with public code.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not quote numeric merge accuracy. Proposal-based sampling can miss true joins that are not adjacent under the oversegmentation. ‘Imitating human proofreading’ is a workflow analogy, not a guarantee of human-level error profiles.

plain_language_summary: Computers often chop a single nerve cell into many pieces in electron-microscope volumes. This method looks at both the overall 3D shape and the zoomed-in image at possible join points to decide which pieces belong together, copying how a person proofreads.

ocar.opportunity: Brain-scale EM reconstructions of nuclei are riddled with split and merge errors in dense tissue. Fixing them without pairwise-only logic would unlock morphology that current correction tools miss.
ocar.challenge: Local pairwise fragment matching cannot recover global cluster topology or missing shape, and manual error labels for training are scarce.
ocar.action: Wang et al. (bioRxiv, 2026) introduced NuGraph, which decomposes bad masks into 3D primitives, reasons with graph attention over whole clusters, aligns primitives to nucleus-level semantics with a contrastive loss, and restores shape via a signed-distance refinement net. A self-supervised engine synthesizes realistic errors. They curated NucEMFix, a brain-wide benchmark on FAFB and MICrONS with more than 8,000 annotated error nuclei.
ocar.resolution: NuGraph reached 87.99% F1 on NucEMFix-F (FAFB) and 86.20% on NucEMFix-M (MICrONS), beating re-segmentation (e.g., +8.6% over nnU-Net) and pairwise correction, while reducing curation effort by over 100× versus manual proofreading.
ocar.future_work: Code and NucEMFix are released to benchmark future global-reasoning correctors on other EM nuclei.

summaries.beginner: Cell nuclei in huge electron-microscope brain maps are often cut into the wrong pieces. A method that looks at all the pieces in a crowded clump at once, rather than two at a time, fixed many of those errors and cut down manual cleanup dramatically.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), Wang, Wei and colleagues present NuGraph for 3D nucleus segmentation correction. Erroneous masks are split into primitives; a point-cloud backbone plus graph attention reasons over entire clusters; a contrastive loss aligns primitives with nucleus-level semantics; a shape network predicts signed distance fields. Trained with synthesized errors, NuGraph scores 87.99% F1 on NucEMFix-FAFB and 86.20% on NucEMFix-MICrONS (8,000+ annotated error nuclei), with >100× less curation than manual proofreading.
summaries.advanced: F1 is on a curated error-case benchmark, not on all nuclei in FAFB/MICrONS. Self-supervised error synthesis may not match every real failure mode. The 100× curation reduction is versus manual proofreading as reported by the authors. Pairwise methods fail on global topology by design; remaining errors likely concentrate on missing morphology the SDF stage cannot invent.

plain_language_summary: Cell nuclei in huge electron-microscope brain maps are often cut into the wrong pieces. A method that looks at all the pieces in a crowded clump at once, rather than two at a time, fixed many of those errors and cut down manual cleanup dramatically.

ocar.opportunity: Taste drives feeding, foraging, and social behavior, yet gustation is among the least mapped senses at connectome scale. A contiguous EM volume covering brain, cervical connective, and ventral nerve cord can close that gap in adult male Drosophila.
ocar.challenge: Gustatory receptor neurons arise in peripheral organs and must be followed into distributed motor, endocrine, and courtship circuits; existing datasets did not span that full path.
ocar.action: Tastekin et al. (bioRxiv, 2025) fully reconstructed male GRNs in that contiguous volume, integrated prior datasets into a pan-CNS cross-sex connectome, clustered GRNs by connectivity, molecular identity, and sexual dimorphism, mapped feeding motor neurons, and traced sensory-to-motor paths.
ocar.resolution: The map revealed distinct circuits for nutrient assessment, motor control, neuroendocrine regulation, and courtship, providing a synaptic-resolution organization of the gustatory system and a framework for how internal state could modulate sensory-driven decisions.
ocar.future_work: The framework is explicitly for studying state-dependent modulation of these sensory-to-motor paths.

summaries.beginner: Scientists reconstructed the fruit fly’s taste nerves all the way from the mouthparts into the brain and nerve cord. The wiring splits into separate paths for judging food, moving mouthparts, hormones, and courtship.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2025), Tastekin, Jefferis, Ribeiro and colleagues present a complete male Drosophila adult gustatory wiring diagram, reconstructing GRNs from peripheral organs through a contiguous EM volume of brain, cervical connective, and VNC (linked to FANC/MANC). Merging existing datasets yielded a pan-CNS, cross-sex connectome. Connectivity clustering, molecular identity, and dimorphism analyses, plus feeding motor-neuron maps, revealed distinct circuits for nutrient assessment, motor control, neuroendocrine regulation, and courtship.
summaries.advanced: The primary reconstruction is male; cross-sex comparison uses integrated existing datasets. ‘Complete’ refers to labellar/proboscis GRNs in this volume, not every taste organ necessarily. Internal-state modulation is a framework, not measured here.

plain_language_summary: Scientists reconstructed the fruit fly’s taste nerves all the way from the mouthparts into the brain and nerve cord. The wiring splits into separate paths for judging food, moving mouthparts, hormones, and courtship.

ocar.opportunity: Canonical circuits for heading, navigation, and orientation have synaptic symmetries tied to the variables they compute. Finding those symmetries in a real connectome would reveal latent variables and responsible cell types.
ocar.challenge: Standard graph embeddings mix cell-type structure with the continuous symmetries one actually wants to see.
ocar.action: Shan and Litwin-Kumar (bioRxiv, 2025) developed a graph embedding that segregates cell-type structure from rotational/translational symmetries, applying it to the adult Drosophila brain connectome and to a synthetic medial-entorhinal grid-cell connectome.
ocar.resolution: The method recovered rotational and translational symmetries in fly heading-direction and visual-projection circuits, and toroidal symmetry in the synthetic grid-cell network. Embedding geometry indicated which latent variables a circuit processes and which cell types implement the computation.
ocar.future_work: The algorithm could be run on other identified circuits whose tuning variables are unknown a priori.

summaries.beginner: Some brain circuits are wired as if they were arranged around a circle or a map. A new embedding method peels that hidden geometry out of a fly wiring diagram without confusing it with ordinary cell-type clustering.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2025), Shan and Litwin-Kumar introduce a graph embedding that separates cell-type structure from computational symmetries. In an adult Drosophila connectome it recovered rotational and translational symmetries in heading-direction and visual projection neuron circuits; in a synthetic medial-entorhinal grid-cell connectome it recovered toroidal symmetry. The embeddings are interpreted as latent variables plus the cell types that process them.
