summaries.advanced: Grid-cell toroidal symmetry is shown on a synthetic connectome, not EM. Success on known fly circuits does not guarantee discovery of unknown variables. Distinguishing cell type from symmetry depends on the segregation step working; residual mixing could invent spurious geometry.

plain_language_summary: Some brain circuits are wired as if they were arranged around a circle or a map. A new embedding method peels that hidden geometry out of a fly wiring diagram without confusing it with ordinary cell-type clustering.

ocar.opportunity: Survival-critical circuits are increasingly viewed as products of genomic decompression. A differentiable map from genes to synapses would let one optimize genetic programs that pre-wire biological agents for tasks.
ocar.challenge: There has been no mechanistic, gradient-friendly account of synaptic multiplicity from gene expression and protein-interaction probabilities.
ocar.action: Boccato, Ferrante, and Toschi (2024) introduced SynaptoGen, a connectome-model member in which synaptic weights equal average synapse counts times conductance derived from genetic profiles, enabling gradient-based search for expression patterns.
ocar.resolution: In simulated synaptogenesis, agents solved four reinforcement-learning benchmarks and consistently beat control baselines. The authors note remaining gaps in biological realism.
ocar.future_work: They argue the framework could accelerate synthetic biological intelligence if those realism gaps are mitigated.

summaries.beginner: This paper offers a computer model that links gene activity to how many synapses form between cells, then tunes those genes so a simulated nervous system can learn simple tasks. The simulated agents beat stripped-down controls, but the authors say the biology is still simplified.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2024 paper (no journal listed), Boccato et al. present SynaptoGen, a differentiable connectome model in which weights are mean synapse counts times conductance from genetic profiles and protein-interaction probabilities. Gradient-based optimization generates expression patterns that pre-wire agents. Validation in simulated synaptogenesis showed success on four reinforcement-learning benchmarks above control baselines, with acknowledged biological-realism gaps.
summaries.advanced: All validation is in simulation; no wet-lab synaptogenesis is shown. ‘Four RL benchmarks’ are unnamed in the abstract. Differentiability buys optimization at the cost of the very stochasticity of real synapse formation. Gaps in realism are explicitly flagged.

plain_language_summary: This paper offers a computer model that links gene activity to how many synapses form between cells, then tunes those genes so a simulated nervous system can learn simple tasks. The simulated agents beat stripped-down controls, but the authors say the biology is still simplified.

ocar.opportunity: Inferring synapses from spike trains would scale circuit mapping beyond paired physiology, but success is controversial.
ocar.challenge: Reconstruction quality depends on dynamical regime, connection type, and recording length, and many algorithms miss inhibition. Ground truth is rare.
ocar.action: Donner et al. (bioRxiv, 2024) compared algorithms on synthetic data and on parallel patch-clamp plus high-density MEA recordings in vitro, then trained an ensemble ANN (eANN) on validated outputs of six established methods.
ocar.resolution: Performance varied strongly with regularity of spontaneous activity, connectivity type, and data duration; inhibitory detection was often weak. The eANN improved accuracy and robustness across regimes, with shorter recordings, especially for inhibition, and improved topological characterization. SHAP analysis of inputs is provided in the author summary.
ocar.future_work: The framework is meant to keep raising inference performance as more multimodal ground truth appears.

summaries.beginner: People try to guess which nerve cells are wired together from the timing of their spikes alone, but the guesses are often wrong, especially for silencing connections. Combining several guessers in a trained ensemble, checked against simultaneous electrode and pipette recordings, improved those guesses.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2024), Donner, Schröter and colleagues benchmark synaptic inference from spike trains using simulations and parallel patch-clamp/HD-MEA ground truth. Accuracy depended on dynamical regime, connection type, and spike-train duration; many algorithms struggled with inhibition. An ensemble ANN trained on six established methods improved robustness across regimes and with shorter recordings, particularly for inhibitory links, and better captured topology.
summaries.advanced: Ground truth is in vitro (three patch cells in parallel with HD-MEA per the author summary), not in vivo cortex. Ensemble gains may not transfer to very different firing statistics. SHAP explains the eANN, not biology. Controversy about spike-train connectomes is acknowledged rather than closed.

plain_language_summary: People try to guess which nerve cells are wired together from the timing of their spikes alone, but the guesses are often wrong, especially for silencing connections. Combining several guessers in a trained ensemble, checked against simultaneous electrode and pipette recordings, improved those guesses.

ocar.opportunity: Fiber (fibration) symmetries in a connectome predict which neurons can synchronize. C. elegans locomotion subnetworks are small enough to compare fibrations with stricter orbit symmetries.
ocar.challenge: How structure yields function in the worm remains unclear, and real connectivity is not ideal.
ocar.action: Avila et al. (PLoS ONE, 2024) searched graph symmetries in symmetrized forward and backward locomotive subnetworks, simulated ODEs admissible to those graphs, compared fiber versus orbit symmetries, and decomposed graphs into nested-loop/multilayer fiber building blocks.
ocar.resolution: Fiber symmetries accurately predicted neuronal synchronization in simulations even under non-idealized connectivity, provided dynamics stayed in stable regimes. Building blocks were nested loops or multilayered fibers.
ocar.future_work: The fiber decomposition offers units to test with calcium imaging or ablation in actual locomotion.

summaries.beginner: If two worm cells sit in matching wiring roles, they may fire together. This study uses a kind of network symmetry to predict those groups in crawling circuits and checks the predictions in simulations.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS ONE (2024), Avila, Makse and colleagues analyze fibration symmetries in symmetrized C. elegans forward and backward locomotive subnetworks, comparing them with more restrictive orbit symmetries. They simulate ordinary differential equations admissible to those graphs. Fiber symmetries predicted synchrony even with imperfect connectivity when dynamics remained stable, and the graphs decomposed into nested-loop or multilayer fiber units.
summaries.advanced: Analyses use symmetrized versions of subnetworks, not the raw directed connectome. Predictions are from ODE simulations, not worm recordings. Stability of the dynamical regime is a precondition. Orbit symmetries being more restrictive means fiber-predicted clusters can be larger than group-theoretic orbits.

plain_language_summary: If two worm cells sit in matching wiring roles, they may fire together. This study uses a kind of network symmetry to predict those groups in crawling circuits and checks the predictions in simulations.

ocar.opportunity: A complete synaptic map of a circadian clock would show how diverse rhythms are orchestrated. FlyWire makes a whole-animal clock connectome possible.
ocar.challenge: The canonical Drosophila clock was counted at about 150 neurons, and monosynaptic links to behavioral and neuroendocrine targets appeared sparse, leaving peptide signaling under-mapped.
ocar.action: Reinhard et al. (bioRxiv, 2024; Nature Communications DOI on record) built a comprehensive clock connectivity map in FlyWire, integrated single-cell transcriptomics and receptor mapping, and searched indirect light inputs.
ocar.resolution: They identified additional dorsal clock neurons, raising the network to about 240 rather than 150 cells, found extensive contralateral synapses, and discovered novel indirect light-input paths. Monosynaptic output to higher-order and neurosecretory cells was sparse, while transcriptomics suggested additional clock neuropeptides and peptide signaling that enriches interconnectivity.
ocar.future_work: Receptor mapping implies functional tests of those putative peptidergic links.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly clock cells keep daily time, but their full wiring was incomplete. Using a whole-brain map, researchers found more clock cells than textbooks listed, lots of left–right connections, and signs that chemical messengers, not just synapses, tie the clock together.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2024), Reinhard, Yoshii, Zandawala and colleagues generated a Drosophila circadian-clock connectome in FlyWire. Additional dorsal neurons raise the count from ~150 to ~240. They report extensive contralateral connectivity, novel indirect light inputs, sparse monosynaptic output to higher-order and neurosecretory cells, and transcriptomic evidence for additional clock neuropeptides that may enrich network interconnectivity.
summaries.advanced: The ~240 count includes newly identified dorsal neurons; classification criteria matter. Peptidergic links are inferred from expression and receptors, not EM synapses. Sparse monosynaptic output could still be functionally strong. Light-input paths are anatomical until physiology confirms.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly clock cells keep daily time, but their full wiring was incomplete. Using a whole-brain map, researchers found more clock cells than textbooks listed, lots of left–right connections, and signs that chemical messengers, not just synapses, tie the clock together.

ocar.opportunity: Temperature cues reach circadian networks and reshape sleep and wake, but the integration circuit in Drosophila was unclear. FlyWire EM can name the nodes.
ocar.challenge: How peripheral temperature neurons join clock cells to retune evening activity and sleep remains incomplete.
ocar.action: Yuan, Li, and Guo (PLoS Biology, 2024) used the FlyWire EM connectome plus genetics, behavior, optogenetic calcium imaging, and peptide-receptor manipulations.
ocar.resolution: Lateral posterior neurons (LPNs) integrate clock and temperature-sensing input and promote sleep. Downstream of thermo-sensitive anterior cells, LPNs suppress activity-promoting LNds via AstC; disrupting LPN–LNd AstC signaling impaired heat-induced reduction of the evening activity peak. Cold-activated LNds stimulate LPNs via NPF–NPFR, a negative-feedback loop that caps LNd activation and fine-tunes the evening peak in the cold.
ocar.future_work: The LPN-centered connectome is a template for other sensory–circadian integrations.

summaries.beginner: Flies sleep differently when it is hot or cold. A wiring-and-behavior study finds a small group of clock-related cells that collect temperature news and, through chemical messengers, turn evening activity up or down.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Biology (2024), Yuan, Li, and Guo map temperature–circadian integration in Drosophila with FlyWire EM. LPNs receive clock and thermosensory input and promote sleep. AC→LPN→LNd suppression via Allatostatin C is needed for heat to cut the evening activity peak (AstCR1 RNAi or mutant). Cold-activated LNds excite LPNs via NPF–NPFR, forming negative feedback that limits the cold-induced evening-peak increase.
summaries.advanced: Causal peptide tests (RNAi, mutant, optogenetics) support the two limbs, but the full connectome neighborhood of LPNs is richer than the highlighted loop. Behavioral readouts are evening activity peaks, not a complete sleep-stage analysis in the abstract. EM connectivity is from the FlyWire brain, not necessarily the same individuals as the behavior.

plain_language_summary: Flies sleep differently when it is hot or cold. A wiring-and-behavior study finds a small group of clock-related cells that collect temperature news and, through chemical messengers, turn evening activity up or down.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic image stacks now reach tera- to petabyte scale with large appearance shifts across regions and samples. Domain adaptation methods from natural images could help synapse detectors generalize.
ocar.challenge: Manual synapse labels are tiny relative to test volumes—often smaller than 0.001% of test data—and out-of-domain connectomics benchmarks have been lacking, so adaptation methods were under-evaluated.
ocar.action: Wu et al. (arXiv, 2023) pose an out-of-domain synapse detection challenge for microwasp brain connectomes to fill that benchmark gap.
ocar.resolution: The abstract states the problem and motivation; it does not report a winning accuracy. The contribution is a challenge setting for evaluating domain adaptation/generalization on connectomic synapses.
ocar.future_work: The challenge is meant to let existing domain-adaptation methods be scored on these out-of-domain wasp volumes.

summaries.beginner: Computers trained to spot synapses in one insect brain often fail on another that looks different, and there has been little shared homework for that problem. This paper sets up such a test using microwasp brain images.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2023), Wu, Wei, Chklovskii and colleagues describe an out-of-domain synapse detection challenge for microwasp brain connectomes. Connectomic stacks are tera- to petabyte scale with diverse appearance, while labels can be <0.001% of test data. Domain-adaptation methods common in natural images lacked a connectomics OOD benchmark; this challenge supplies one.
summaries.advanced: No performance numbers are given. The <0.001% figure is a scale illustration of the label/test mismatch. Success on wasp brains may not transfer to vertebrate EM. Challenge papers should not be read as completed method papers.

plain_language_summary: Computers trained to spot synapses in one insect brain often fail on another that looks different, and there has been little shared homework for that problem. This paper sets up such a test using microwasp brain images.

ocar.opportunity: Edge AI still needs data-efficient, power-efficient, generalizable learners. Large neuroimaging and synapse-resolution maps could constrain machine-learning architectures rather than merely inspire slogans.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear which biological motifs actually improve robustness or continual learning when inserted into engineered nets.
ocar.action: Johnson et al. (SPIE Defense + Commercial Sensing, 2023) report a pipeline: motif discovery feeding neural architecture search; analysis of the fly heading circuit for sensor fusion; memory-circuit-inspired generative replay; and mammalian-cortex constraints on transformers.
ocar.resolution: Discovered motifs were evolved into network architectures, and a novel fly heading-direction connectivity pattern supported robotic sensor fusion. Fly memory circuitry inspired a generative-replay method with over 20% accuracy improvement in incremental class learning. Cortical constraints increased robustness on the hardest CIFAR-10-C examples while cutting learnable attention parameters by over an order of magnitude.
ocar.future_work: The four strands are presented as complementary routes to keep mining connectomes for ML inductive biases.

summaries.beginner: This engineering paper tries several ways to steal ideas from real brain wiring to make computer models that learn with less data and power. Copying fly memory circuits and some mammalian cortex wiring rules improved specific learning and robustness tests.
summaries.intermediate: At Defense + Commercial Sensing (2023), Johnson, Gray Roncal, Wester and colleagues describe several connectome-constrained AI efforts. Motif discovery fed a neural architecture search, and a fly heading-direction circuit with a newly noted connectivity pattern was demonstrated for sensor fusion on a robot. A generative-replay method inspired by fly memory circuitry improved incremental class-learning accuracy by more than 20%, while cortex-inspired transformer constraints improved CIFAR-10-C robustness and cut learnable attention parameters by over tenfold.
summaries.advanced: Gains are task-specific (incremental class learning; CIFAR-10-C hard examples) and not a general law. ‘Novel’ heading connectivity is used in a model plus robot demo, not a full proof of biological sufficiency. Parameter reduction in attention is an efficiency claim that still depends on the unmodified transformer baseline.

plain_language_summary: This engineering paper tries several ways to steal ideas from real brain wiring to make computer models that learn with less data and power. Copying fly memory circuits and some mammalian cortex wiring rules improved specific learning and robustness tests.

ocar.opportunity: Super-resolution light microscopy sees chosen molecules but not dense tissue context, which synapse-level circuit mapping needs. A light-based dense map of chemically fixed brain—including human clinical samples—would complement EM.
ocar.challenge: Optical methods have not comprehensively delineated cellular architecture from millimeter regions down to nanometer synaptic clefts in diverse fixed preparations.
ocar.action: Michalska et al. (Nature Biotechnology, 2023) developed CATS: fixation-compatible extracellular labeling plus STED or expansion microscopy, applied to rodent and human tissue including FFPE diagnostics, and to mouse hippocampal mossy-fiber circuitry.
ocar.resolution: CATS enabled 3D reconstruction of single synapses and mapping of putative synaptic clefts. In mossy fiber circuitry they reconstructed and quantified synaptic input and output of identified neurons. The method worked on clinically derived human samples.
ocar.future_work: Applicability to diagnostic specimens suggests use in disease architecture studies, with putative clefts still needing EM or physiology cross-checks where claims are synaptic.

summaries.beginner: New light-microscope labeling can outline almost every cell in a piece of brain, not just a few glowing ones, down to likely contact points between cells. The method works in mouse hippocampus and in stored human brain samples.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Biotechnology (2023), Michalska, Danzl and colleagues introduce CATS: extracellular labeling compatible with chemical fixation, imaged with STED or expansion microscopy from millimeter to nanometer scales. They apply it to rodent and human brain, including formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded diagnostic specimens. The method reconstructs single synapses via putative cleft regions and quantifies mossy-fiber input and output of identified mouse hippocampal neurons.
summaries.advanced: Synapses are identified as putative cleft regions optically, not by EM vesicle/PSD gold standards. Expansion/STED still require dense labeling quality. Human FFPE demonstration is architectural visualization; disease interpretation is prospective. Extracellular label access may vary by region and fixation.

plain_language_summary: New light-microscope labeling can outline almost every cell in a piece of brain, not just a few glowing ones, down to likely contact points between cells. The method works in mouse hippocampus and in stored human brain samples.

ocar.opportunity: The insect central complex is a conserved navigation hub, yet species occupy wildly different sensory worlds. Developmental lineages that build CX input channels may explain how an invariant structure absorbs novelty.
ocar.challenge: Without overlaying lineage tracts on a synapse-scale connectome, it is hard to see which input channels are lineage-specific and therefore evolvable modules.
ocar.action: Kandimalla, Omoto, Hong, and Hartenstein (Journal of Comparative Physiology, 2023) mapped CX input channels onto the Drosophila hemibrain connectome using developmental tract identity, integrating anatomy and physiology from other insects.
ocar.resolution: They observed neuropil- and lineage-specific innervation, connectivity, and activity profiles. They argue that neuroblast proliferative potential and lineage-based channels allow species-specific modification of existing, novel, or deprecated modalities—a substrate for evolving navigational circuits.
ocar.future_work: Comparative physiology across insects can test whether lineage modules predict ecological specializations.

summaries.beginner: Insects share a brain region that helps them navigate, even though they live very different lives. This review-style analysis ties the fruit-fly wiring of that region to the developmental families of cells that build its input lines, suggesting evolution can retune those families without redesigning the whole hub.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Comparative Physiology (2023), Kandimalla et al. examine central-complex input channels in developmental and evolutionary context. Overlaying lineage tracts on the Drosophila hemibrain connectome, and integrating other species’ anatomy and physiology, they find neuropil- and lineage-specific innervation, connectivity, and activity. Lineage architecture plus neuroblast proliferation is proposed as the substrate for species-specific navigational diversification.
summaries.advanced: Hemibrain is one female brain region, not all insects. Activity profiles drawn from other species are not simultaneous with the EM. The evolutionary mechanism is a hypothesis linking development to ecology, not a phylogenetic reconstruction in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Insects share a brain region that helps them navigate, even though they live very different lives. This review-style analysis ties the fruit-fly wiring of that region to the developmental families of cells that build its input lines, suggesting evolution can retune those families without redesigning the whole hub.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila mushroom body compartments assign valence in parallel, but how those abstract values become actions such as walking upwind is poorly understood.
ocar.challenge: Memory retrieval must convert compartment-specific MBON signals into oriented movement without a known integrator.
ocar.action: Aso et al. (eLife, 2023) measured upwind locomotion after appetitive memories in different compartments, photoactivated a new split-GAL4 collection, and used EM connectomics to find neurons postsynaptic to MBONs.
ocar.resolution: Different compartments induced different amounts of upwind locomotion. UpWind Neurons (UpWiNs) integrate inhibitory appetitive-compartment and excitatory aversive-compartment MBON input, gain odor responses after appetitive learning as the inhibitory MBON depresses, are required for appetitive memory and upwind retrieval, and also promote return to a location where activation ended.
ocar.future_work: The divergent-then-convergent architecture is offered as a general motif for turning learned valence into action.

summaries.beginner: When a fly learns that a smell predicts sugar, it later walks upwind toward that smell. Researchers found a cluster of cells that collect like-and-dislike signals from the learning center and turn them into that upwind walk.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2023), Aso, Hige and colleagues show that appetitive memories stored in different Drosophila mushroom-body compartments drive different levels of upwind locomotion. EM connectomics and a split-GAL4 photoactivation screen identified UpWind Neurons that mix inhibitory (appetitive) and excitatory (aversive) MBON inputs. After appetitive learning, UpWiNs respond more to the rewarded odor as the inhibitory MBON depresses; blocking them impairs memory and upwind retrieval; activating them also increases return to the shutoff location.
summaries.advanced: Upwind locomotion is one action component of retrieval, not all learned behavior. Photoactivation screens can miss redundant parallel paths. EM partners are from a reference brain, not the imaged flies. The ‘return to location’ effect suggests a navigation role beyond valence readout.

plain_language_summary: When a fly learns that a smell predicts sugar, it later walks upwind toward that smell. Researchers found a cluster of cells that collect like-and-dislike signals from the learning center and turn them into that upwind walk.

ocar.opportunity: Many animals navigate toward unseen goals using internal spatial maps. Arthropod systems, especially Drosophila with a connectome, have clarified attractor networks anchored to landmarks and tied to motor control.
ocar.challenge: Anatomical synapses are not the functional graph: which synapses are active appears to be continually reselected.
ocar.action: Wilson (Annual Review of Neuroscience, 2023) synthesizes navigation networks from connections to computations, with emphasis on arthropods and the fly connectome plus plasticity.
ocar.resolution: Maps are organized around attractor dynamics, landmark anchoring, and reciprocal motor links. Functional synapses seem continually chosen from anatomical potential synapses via Hebbian rules, sensory feedback, attractor dynamics, and neuromodulation—explaining rapid map updates and how goals can be initialized as stable fixed points.
ocar.future_work: The review highlights plasticity-in-connectomes as the next experimental priority rather than more static wiring alone.

summaries.beginner: Animals can head toward a hidden goal using an internal map. This review explains how insect brains appear to keep those maps as stable activity patterns that are tied to landmarks and movement, and how the working connections can change quickly even if the anatomical wires stay put.
summaries.intermediate: In Annual Review of Neuroscience (2023), Rachel I. Wilson reviews navigation networks from connectivity to computation, focusing on arthropods and Drosophila. Spatial maps are attractor networks anchored to landmarks and reciprocally linked to motor control. She argues functional synapses are continually reselected from anatomical potential synapses by Hebbian learning, sensory feedback, attractor dynamics, and neuromodulation, enabling rapid map updates and goal initialization as stable fixed points.
summaries.advanced: The reselection thesis is a synthesis, not a single new experiment. Connectomes constrain potential synapses; physiology is still required to see the active subset. Transfer from arthropod compasses to mammalian maps is suggested by shared attractor language, not proven here.

plain_language_summary: Animals can head toward a hidden goal using an internal map. This review explains how insect brains appear to keep those maps as stable activity patterns that are tied to landmarks and movement, and how the working connections can change quickly even if the anatomical wires stay put.

ocar.opportunity: Neuromodulation is often treated as uniform within a cell class. Heterogeneous serotonin receptor expression inside Drosophila olfactory projection neurons could instead tune different odor channels differently.
ocar.challenge: If receptor co-expression varies within PNs, class-level 5-HT stories will miss stimulus-specific modulation.
ocar.action: Jonaitis et al. (bioRxiv, 2023) mapped 5-HT receptor co-expression in two PN populations, compared glomerular innervation and downstream convergence in a connectome, and measured odor-evoked responses under 5-HT.
ocar.resolution: Both PN populations heterogeneously co-expressed all 5-HT receptors. Distinct receptor-defined PN sets innervated different glomerular combinations and showed little downstream convergence. 5-HT differentially modulated odor-evoked responses according to receptor profile and odor tuning.
ocar.future_work: Heterogeneous receptor maps predict that modulation should be reinterpreted per odor scene, not per nominal cell class.

summaries.beginner: Brain chemicals like serotonin are often assumed to affect a whole cell type the same way. In fly smell cells, different cells of the same broad type carry different serotonin receptors, and serotonin then changes their odor responses in different ways.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2023), Jonaitis, Dacks and colleagues show that two Drosophila olfactory projection-neuron populations heterogeneously co-express all 5-HT receptors. Receptor-defined PN groups innervate different glomerular combinations, and connectomics indicates little convergence onto shared downstream partners. Serotonin differentially modulates odor-evoked PN responses according to receptor profile and odor tuning.
summaries.advanced: ‘All 5-HT receptors’ co-expression is at population level with heterogeneity, not every cell expressing every receptor. Downstream ‘little convergence’ is connectomic, not functional. Modulation differences are odor-evoked; spontaneous or other-state effects are not in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Brain chemicals like serotonin are often assumed to affect a whole cell type the same way. In fly smell cells, different cells of the same broad type carry different serotonin receptors, and serotonin then changes their odor responses in different ways.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans synapse biology is rich, but quantifying fluorescent synapse markers across many animals, ages, and sexes is slow and biased. A general image pipeline plus a strain resource would scale that anatomy.
ocar.challenge: Neurite morphology, fluorescence, and imaging parameters vary enormously, so one detector often fails.
ocar.action: Majeed et al. (bioRxiv, 2023) present WormPsyQi, an automated pipeline for synaptically localized fluorescent signals, plus 30 transgenic strains labeling chemical or electrical synapses (CLA-1, RAB-3, GRASP, innexins).
ocar.resolution: WormPsyQi captured synaptic structures despite heterogeneity and quantified number, size, intensity, and spatial distribution across nervous-system regions, stages, and sexes. The authors note it can extend to other punctate signals (receptors, CAMs).
ocar.future_work: The toolkit is positioned to expand sample size and phenotypic space for C. elegans synapse genetics without EM for every experiment.

summaries.beginner: Counting tiny fluorescent synapses in worms by hand is slow and inconsistent. This paper offers software plus a set of labeled worm strains that automatically measure synapse number, size, and placement across ages and sexes.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2023), Majeed, Hobert, Lu and colleagues introduce WormPsyQi to automatically quantify synaptic fluorescent signals in C. elegans. They also release 30 strains marking chemical or electrical synapses via CLA-1, RAB-3, GRASP, or innexins. The pipeline handled diverse neurite shapes and imaging settings and reported synapse number, size, intensity, and distribution across regions, stages, and sexes.
summaries.advanced: Fluorescent puncta are not EM-verified synapses in this abstract. GRASP/iBLINC-style labels have known false-positive/negative modes. ‘Reduced human bias’ is relative to manual scoring. Extension to receptors/CAMs is proposed.

plain_language_summary: Counting tiny fluorescent synapses in worms by hand is slow and inconsistent. This paper offers software plus a set of labeled worm strains that automatically measure synapse number, size, and placement across ages and sexes.

ocar.opportunity: Synapse sign—excitatory versus inhibitory—is essential for brain models but hard to map. Computational inference could fill C. elegans gaps under several data regimes.
ocar.challenge: Available data may include expression plus wiring rules, expression plus some known signs, or neither.
ocar.action: Harris, Wytock, and Kovács (Advanced Science, 2022) present three methods: a connectome model (CM) using neurotransmitter and receptor expression with a wiring-rule network; a spatial CM trained with known polarities; and a generalized CM treating remaining signs as network sign prediction.
ocar.resolution: CM resolved 356 polarities beyond 1,752 known. Spatial CM recovered 81% of CM-resolved connections at >95% precision and inferred 147 additional unknown polarities. Generalized CM is offered for the no-expression case, with reported high performance.
ocar.future_work: The suite is aimed at unveiling large-scale polarities as inputs to more realistic dynamics models.

summaries.beginner: Knowing whether a worm connection is a push or a pull is hard to measure everywhere. Using gene-expression clues and the known wiring, this work predicts many of those signs and checks them against the signs already known.
summaries.intermediate: In Advanced Science (2022), Harris, Wytock, and Kovács infer C. elegans synaptic polarities in three data regimes. A connectome model combining neurotransmitter/receptor expression with wiring rules resolved 356 signs beyond 1,752 known. A spatial model trained on known polarities recovered 81% of those CM-resolved links at >95% precision and added 147 more. A generalized CM handles the no-expression, no-rule case as sign prediction.
summaries.advanced: Resolved polarities are computational, not new electrophysiology. Precision >95% is for recovering CM-resolved (already model-based) connections, a slightly circular gold set. Generalized CM performance is asserted as high without a number in that sentence. NT–R wiring rules may be incomplete.

plain_language_summary: Knowing whether a worm connection is a push or a pull is hard to measure everywhere. Using gene-expression clues and the known wiring, this work predicts many of those signs and checks them against the signs already known.

ocar.opportunity: EM and X-ray microtomography can seed the next generation of submicron brain atlases, but only if annotations travel between groups.
ocar.challenge: Collection, annotation, and storage practices vary, limiting comparative and secondary analysis even when spatial image interfaces are improving.
ocar.action: Sanchez et al. (Frontiers in Neuroinformatics, 2022) share design considerations and a use case for standardizing connectomics annotation metadata, especially for neuroanatomical entities.
ocar.resolution: They argue standardization will enable validation, sharing, and replication, amplifying community investment. A use case from a recent large-scale dataset is developed.
ocar.future_work: Adoption of a common metadata schema is the practical next step the paper is advocating.

summaries.beginner: Huge brain-image projects each invent their own way to name and store the notes on cells and connections. This paper argues for a shared metadata language so those notes can be compared and reused.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2022), Sanchez, Gray Roncal, Lichtman and colleagues address variability in connectomics annotation metadata despite progress on large-scale spatial image interfaces. They present design considerations and a use case from a recent large dataset. The aim is to standardize neuroanatomical entity metadata for validation, sharing, and replication.
summaries.advanced: This is a standards/use-case paper, not a new reconstruction. Impact depends on community adoption. The abstract does not specify a schema version or ontology alignment details.

plain_language_summary: Huge brain-image projects each invent their own way to name and store the notes on cells and connections. This paper argues for a shared metadata language so those notes can be compared and reused.

ocar.opportunity: Connection strengths in neuronal networks are heavy-tailed across species, but a simple generative mechanism has been missing.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear whether heavy tails require species-specific biology or follow from generic self-organization.
ocar.action: Lynn, Holmes, and Palmer (bioRxiv, 2022) proposed a minimal model: random pruning plus synaptic-strength rearrangement mixing preferential and random growth, then extended it with activity and Hebbian plasticity.
ocar.resolution: Networks evolved asymptotically scale-free strength distributions whose exponent depended only on the probability of preferential versus random growth. Adding Hebbian plasticity produced clustering. Predictions matched connectomes of several animals, suggesting heavy-tailed, clustered connectivity can arise from general self-organization.
ocar.future_work: The species-generality claim invites tests on new connectomes and on whether measured preferential-growth probabilities predict exponents.

summaries.beginner: In many animals a few nerve-cell connections are much stronger than the rest. A simple model where synapses are randomly trimmed and remaining strengths grow either at random or ‘the rich get richer’ can produce that pattern, and adding a fire-together-wire-together rule also creates clusters.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2022), Lynn, Holmes, and Palmer explain heavy-tailed neuronal connection strengths with a minimal self-organization model: random pruning plus mixed preferential/random strength growth. The asymptotic strength distribution is scale-free with an exponent set only by the preferential-growth probability. Including activity and Hebbian plasticity yields clustering. They report confirmation in several animal connectomes.
summaries.advanced: ‘Several animals’ are not named in the abstract body (the lead says four species). Scale-free tails are asymptotic; finite connectomes can look similar under other tails. Preferential growth is a statistical mechanism, not a identified molecular rule. Clustering from Hebbian extension is model-side until quantified per species.

plain_language_summary: In many animals a few nerve-cell connections are much stronger than the rest. A simple model where synapses are randomly trimmed and remaining strengths grow either at random or ‘the rich get richer’ can produce that pattern, and adding a fire-together-wire-together rule also creates clusters.

ocar.opportunity: Multisensory integration is central to behavior but poorly understood at molecular, synaptic, and circuit levels. C. elegans, with a mapped connectome and simple nervous system, can supply those levels, then be compared with mammals.
ocar.challenge: Mammalian MSI is hard to reduce to identified cells; worm studies are scattered across convergence sites.
ocar.action: Yu, Xue, and Chen (Brain Sciences, 2022) review representative C. elegans MSI cases where convergence occurs at sensory neurons or interneurons, and compare mechanisms with mammals.
ocar.resolution: They argue the worm yields unique insight into how combining senses produces flexible behavior, and that whole-brain imaging may be crucial for seeing the brain as a whole.
ocar.future_work: Emerging whole-brain imaging is highlighted as the way to move from local convergence anecdotes to system-level MSI.

summaries.beginner: Animals combine senses to make one picture of the world. This review collects examples from the tiny worm, where scientists can watch combination happen in single identified cells, and compares those examples with mammals.
summaries.intermediate: In Brain Sciences (2022), Yu, Xue, and Chen review multisensory integration in C. elegans versus mammals. Worm paradigms include convergence at sensory neurons or at interneurons. They argue the mapped connectome and genetic tools give molecular-to-circuit mechanisms that remain scarce in mammals, and that whole-brain imaging may be needed to treat MSI as a whole-brain function.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review. Homology of mechanisms with mammals is comparative, not evidence of conserved molecules in each cited case. Convergence site (sensory vs interneuron) may not map onto mammalian cortical MSI.

plain_language_summary: Animals combine senses to make one picture of the world. This review collects examples from the tiny worm, where scientists can watch combination happen in single identified cells, and compares those examples with mammals.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans nociceptive circuits use the same neurons in both sexes but wire them differently, a chance to link topology to sexually dimorphic behavior.
ocar.challenge: Sensory responses may be similar even when behavior differs, so the downstream graph—not the sensor—may hold the dimorphism.
ocar.action: Pechuk et al. (Current Biology, 2022) showed similar nociceptive sensory responses but dimorphic behavior, learned network models that replicate the behaviors, predicted simple rewirings that should switch sex-typical behavior, and tested those rewirings experimentally, including mating assays in rewired males.
ocar.resolution: Predicted subtle synaptic rewirings flipped behavior between sexes. Rewired males were worse at finding mates when aversive cues were present, suggesting topologies that support efficient nociceptive avoidance carry a reproductive cost.
ocar.future_work: The deconstruction is a template for reprogramming other dimorphic circuits with small wiring edits.

summaries.beginner: Male and female worms use the same pain-sensing cells but wire them differently, and they behave differently toward nasty stimuli. Changing a few connections was enough to make one sex act more like the other, but in males that change interfered with finding mates.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2022), Pechuk, Oren-Suissa, Schneidman and colleagues study sexually dimorphic nociception in C. elegans: sensory neurons respond similarly, yet behavior differs. Network models fitted to the dimorphic graphs predicted small rewirings that experimentally switched sex-typical behavior. Rewired males were compromised in mate finding amid aversive cues, implying a reproductive cost to avoidance-efficient topologies.
summaries.advanced: Rewirings are ‘simple’ and experimentally successful in the reported assays; completeness of the nociceptive graph still matters. Mate-finding cost is shown for rewired males under aversive cues, not a full fitness landscape. Model uniqueness is not guaranteed: other rewirings might also flip behavior.

plain_language_summary: Male and female worms use the same pain-sensing cells but wire them differently, and they behave differently toward nasty stimuli. Changing a few connections was enough to make one sex act more like the other, but in males that change interfered with finding mates.

ocar.opportunity: Sparse neuron tracing from a seed mask could complement dense EM reconstruction when full volume labeling is unnecessary or too costly. Anisotropic volumes make that tracing hard.
ocar.challenge: Dense-reconstruction methods dominate the literature; sparse tracing with only initial seeds is understudied, and misalignment breaks traces.
ocar.action: Liu et al. (Biomedical Signal Processing and Control, 2021) built an AI system using convolutional LSTMs for inter-slice context, a lightweight U-Net for intra-slice cues, recursive training, and a shift-estimation module.
ocar.resolution: They report the first use of an RNN for neuron tracing in this setting, better performance than other state-of-the-art methods on two highly anisotropic datasets, and longer traces after shift correction.
ocar.future_work: Shift correction suggests applying the tracer to large, imperfectly aligned production volumes.

summaries.beginner: Sometimes scientists only need to follow a few nerve cells through a stack of electron-microscope slices, starting from a small painted seed. A system that remembers nearby slices and fixes jumps from misaligned pictures followed cells farther than prior tools on two tough datasets.
summaries.intermediate: In Biomedical Signal Processing and Control (2021), Liu, Han and colleagues present an AI sparse-tracing system for anisotropic EM volumes. ConvLSTMs estimate inter-slice context, a lightweight U-Net reads intra-slice structure, recursive training improves performance, and shift estimation lengthens traces despite misalignment. They claim a first RNN application to neuron tracing and better results than other state-of-the-art methods on two highly anisotropic datasets.
summaries.advanced: ‘First RNN for neuron tracing’ is the authors’ claim. SOTA is on two unnamed (in the abstract) anisotropic datasets. Sparse tracing from seeds will still fail at true biological branches that look like alignment jumps. Recursive training can overfit seed appearance.

plain_language_summary: Sometimes scientists only need to follow a few nerve cells through a stack of electron-microscope slices, starting from a small painted seed. A system that remembers nearby slices and fixes jumps from misaligned pictures followed cells farther than prior tools on two tough datasets.

ocar.opportunity: Taste neurons tell the brain about calories and toxins, but the synaptic signals they send and receive in the adult fly brain were unmapped at EM scale.
ocar.challenge: Labellar axons might mix modalities or keep them separate; without a reconstruction, axo-axonic interactions stay invisible.
ocar.action: Engert, Sterne, Bock, and Scott (bioRxiv, 2021) reconstructed gustatory axons and synapses in a whole-brain EM volume: 87 labellar projections on the right, 57 on the left.
ocar.resolution: They recovered the majority of labellar gustatory axons. Neurons had nearly equal pre- and postsynaptic sites with extensive axo-axonic connectivity. Morphology- and connectivity-based clustering yielded six groups, likely different taste modalities, and most synapses were within-group.
ocar.future_work: The six-group map is a base for matching molecular taste identities to EM clusters and for testing how within-group synapses reshape transmission.

summaries.beginner: Researchers listed most of the fruit fly’s labellar taste-nerve endings in a whole-brain electron-microscope volume. The nerves clustered into six groups that mostly talk among themselves, as if different tastes are kept on separate lines, yet they also receive many incoming synapses on their own axons.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2021), Engert, Sterne, Bock, and Scott reconstructed 87 right-hemisphere and 57 left-hemisphere Drosophila labellar gustatory projections in a whole-brain EM volume—the majority of labellar GRN axons. Axons bore nearly equal pre- and postsynaptic sites with extensive interconnectivity. Clustering produced six groups, likely taste modalities, with the vast majority of synapses within-group.
summaries.advanced: Left/right counts differ (87 vs 57), so completeness is hemispherically uneven. Modality labels are inferred from clustering, not receptor genetics in this abstract. Nearly equal pre/post counts do not imply equal functional impact. ‘Majority of labellar axons’ is not all gustatory organs.

plain_language_summary: Researchers listed most of the fruit fly’s labellar taste-nerve endings in a whole-brain electron-microscope volume. The nerves clustered into six groups that mostly talk among themselves, as if different tastes are kept on separate lines, yet they also receive many incoming synapses on their own axons.

ocar.opportunity: New technologies in the past two decades have rapidly advanced how circuits are assembled and then stably kept, often for years. EM connectomes, live imaging, omics, and genetic screens now let principles of architecture be stated more sharply.
ocar.challenge: Establishment and lifelong maintenance may obey overlapping but distinct rules that reviews must separate.
ocar.action: Heckman and Doe (Journal of Neuroscience, 2021) review how model-organism connectomes, advanced light microscopy, transcriptomics/proteomics, and high-throughput genetics have expanded the principles governing circuit formation and maintenance.
ocar.resolution: They discuss an expanded set of principles covering stereotyped versus variable connections, cellular dynamics of construction and maintenance, molecular programs, and genetic discovery of wiring regulators.
ocar.future_work: The review frames continued integration of these tools as the way to test which establishment rules also run maintenance.

summaries.beginner: Building a brain circuit and keeping it stable for years are related but not identical jobs. This review gathers new maps, movies of growing cells, gene lists, and genetic screens that have updated the rulebook for both jobs.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience (2021), Heckman and Doe review how neural circuits are established and then stably maintained. They highlight EM connectomes of model organisms, live imaging of construction and maintenance dynamics, transcriptomic and proteomic programs, and high-throughput genetic screens for wiring regulators. Together those tools, they argue, have expanded the principles of circuit architecture over about two decades.
summaries.advanced: Duplicate opening sentences in the abstract signal a review/highlight format rather than new data. Principles are qualitative. EM stereotypy versus variability is species- and region-dependent.

plain_language_summary: Building a brain circuit and keeping it stable for years are related but not identical jobs. This review gathers new maps, movies of growing cells, gene lists, and genetic screens that have updated the rulebook for both jobs.

ocar.opportunity: Mammalian neuromuscular connections reorganize massively after birth. Complete muscle connectomes at successive ages could reveal whether pruning is random or ordered.
ocar.challenge: Without full wiring at birth versus later, one cannot see how much overlap collapses or whether a global ranking governs both local and long-distance competition.
ocar.action: Meirovitch et al. (bioRxiv, 2021) used serial-section SEM at birth, Brainbow reconstructions neonatally, and XFP-based reconstructions in older mouse muscle to trace all connectivity across ages.
ocar.resolution: Axons pruned about 85% of branches in the first two postnatal weeks, with an ~8-fold drop in multi-innervated junctions and a ~6-fold drop in fibers with more than one NMJ. Simplification followed a rank-order co-innervation preference already detectable at birth and still visible in rare adult multi-NMJ fibers, likely reflecting activity similarity and Henneman-like recruitment order. The same ranking governed local and millimeter-scale competitions.
ocar.future_work: The authors interpret the mature map as function (recruitment order) sculpting structure from initially near all-to-all connectivity.

summaries.beginner: Newborn mammals have extra nerve branches on their muscles that are later trimmed away. Mapping those connections as mice grow showed the trimming is not random: nerves that work in a similar ranked order stay together longest.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2021), Meirovitch, Lichtman and colleagues reconstructed mouse neuromuscular connectomes across development with ssSEM at birth plus Brainbow and XFP tracing later. Axons pruned about 85% of branches in two postnatal weeks; multi-innervated junctions fell ~8-fold and fibers with more than one NMJ ~6-fold. Remaining co-innervation followed a rank order present at birth, likely activity-pattern similarity related to Henneman recruitment, applying both inside junctions and millimeters apart.
summaries.advanced: 85%, ~8-fold, and ~6-fold are the abstract’s figures; methods differ by age (SEM vs fluorescence), which can affect completeness. Rank order is inferred from topology and muscle-fiber properties, not simultaneous motor-unit recordings here. ‘Nearly all-to-all’ at birth is relative, not literal complete mixing.

plain_language_summary: Newborn mammals have extra nerve branches on their muscles that are later trimmed away. Mapping those connections as mice grow showed the trimming is not random: nerves that work in a similar ranked order stay together longest.

ocar.opportunity: Platynereis dumerilii is a marine annelid with spiral cleavage, a trochophore larva, and growing use across development, chronobiology, neurobiology, and ecology. Whole-body volume EM and single-cell genomics now make it a connectomics model too.
ocar.challenge: The community needs a single overview of history, current topics, and methods so new groups can enter.
ocar.action: Özpolat et al. (EvoDevo, 2021) review Platynereis as a model, from nineteenth-century embryology to multimodal cellular atlases and rope-ladder CNS reconstructions in the young worm.
ocar.resolution: They survey genetics, regeneration, reproduction, evolution, chronobiology, ecotoxicology, connectomics, and single-cell genomics, aiming to expand the active community.
ocar.future_work: The unique whole-body EM plus atlas combination is presented as the next growth area.

summaries.beginner: The marine worm Platynereis is becoming a standard laboratory animal for development and brain research. This review explains why, including new whole-body electron-microscope maps of its simple ladder-like nervous system.
summaries.intermediate: In EvoDevo (2021), Özpolat, Arendt, Tessmar-Raible, Raible, Jékely and colleagues review Platynereis dumerilii as a rising laboratory model. They trace a history from nineteenth-century eye-development and spiral-cleavage studies to molecular work on growth, hormones, and clocks. The review emphasizes whole-body volume EM and single-cell atlases of the young worm that enable tracing neurons in a rope-ladder central nervous system.
summaries.advanced: This is a community/model-system review, not a connectome paper per se. Volume EM advantages are for the young worm’s size. Comparisons with Drosophila or C. elegans are implicit in the ‘model system’ pitch.

plain_language_summary: The marine worm Platynereis is becoming a standard laboratory animal for development and brain research. This review explains why, including new whole-body electron-microscope maps of its simple ladder-like nervous system.

ocar.opportunity: Huge EM volumes make voxel-wise neuron labeling costly. If the scientific product is a brain graph, path-finding between keypoints may suffice and be cheaper than dense segmentation.
ocar.challenge: State-of-the-art convnet segmentation can be hard to run at scale under schedule and cost limits, and small segmentation errors catastrophically distort connectomes.
ocar.action: Drenkow et al. (bioRxiv, 2020) recast connectivity as autonomous-navigation path-finding: swarms of virtual agents with cheap sensors on potential fields avoid membranes and find synapses, sharing information to sparsely trace paths and capture connectivity, skeletons, and path length.
ocar.resolution: They report meeting or exceeding state-of-the-art performance at substantially lower computational cost, producing a sparse pathway segmentation and connectivity graph.
ocar.future_work: They suggest generalization to bronchial trees or road networks as analogous tracing problems.

summaries.beginner: Instead of painting every voxel of every neuron, this method sends virtual scouts through electron-microscope brain images to find paths between landmarks and synapses. The authors say it builds a useful wiring sketch for less computer time.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Drenkow, Gray Roncal and colleagues treat EM neuron connectivity as path-finding. Virtual agents use local potential-field sensors to avoid membranes and locate synapses, sharing information as a swarm to produce sparse pathway segmentation, skeletons, path lengths, and a connectivity graph. They report SOTA-matching or better results at substantially lower computational cost than convnet-dominated pipelines.
summaries.advanced: ‘Meet or exceed SOTA’ is not numeric in the abstract. Sparse graphs can miss branches the agents never seed. Agent sensors assume membranes and synapses are detectable in the potential field. Comparison fairness depends on whether SOTA was dense instance segmentation (a different output).

plain_language_summary: Instead of painting every voxel of every neuron, this method sends virtual scouts through electron-microscope brain images to find paths between landmarks and synapses. The authors say it builds a useful wiring sketch for less computer time.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans locomotion circuitry is a testbed for how brains generate coordinated motion. Treating the worm as a multilayer network that includes transmitters and peptides may predict which cells belong to that subnetwork.
ocar.challenge: Single-layer graphs omit neuromodulatory coupling that may be essential for gait.
ocar.action: Maertens, Schöll, Ruiz, and Hövel (Neurocomputing, 2020) mapped a multilayer C. elegans network, used logistic regression to predict locomotory subnetwork neurons, coupled Hindmarsh–Rose neural dynamics to a leaky-integrator muscle model and a harmonic-wave body model, and applied time-delayed feedback plus silencing.
ocar.resolution: The pipeline predicted locomotory neurons, simulated forward locomotion, and showed that delayed feedback synchronization contributes to coordination. Silencing neurons in silico ranked their importance for coordinated locomotion.
ocar.future_work: Because they argue information processing is shared with humans, they present the study as insight into how brains generate motion generally.

summaries.beginner: Researchers modeled the worm as stacked networks of different chemical conversation types to guess which cells run crawling. Simulated muscles and a simple wave for the body, plus a feedback trick that lines cells up in time, produced coordinated crawling and ranked cells by how much the gait needed them.
summaries.intermediate: In Neurocomputing (2020), Maertens et al. treat C. elegans as a multilayer network of neurotransmitters and neuropeptides. Logistic regression predicted locomotory-subnetwork neurons. Hindmarsh–Rose neurons, leaky-integrator muscles, and a harmonic-wave body model simulated forward locomotion; time-delayed feedback revealed synchronization contributing to coordination, and in-silico silencing ranked neurons’ importance.
summaries.advanced: Logistic-regression ‘prediction’ of known locomotory neurons can be circular if labels leak. Hindmarsh–Rose plus harmonic waves are highly reduced versus biomechanics. The leap to human motor control is analogical. Delayed feedback is a control probe, not a proven worm mechanism.

plain_language_summary: Researchers modeled the worm as stacked networks of different chemical conversation types to guess which cells run crawling. Simulated muscles and a simple wave for the body, plus a feedback trick that lines cells up in time, produced coordinated crawling and ranked cells by how much the gait needed them.

ocar.opportunity: Single-cell expression and the C. elegans connectome together could reveal genetic rules for who connects to whom, including gap junctions.
ocar.challenge: There have been few experimentally testable computational links from identity to adjacency in the presence of noise and space.
ocar.action: Kovács, Barabási, and Barabási (PNAS record / bioRxiv 2020) introduced a framework relating the connectome adjacency matrix to neuronal expression, accounting for data noise and spatial constraints, and inferred innexin interaction rules for gap junctions.
ocar.resolution: They inferred a network of 19 innexin interactions governing gap-junction formation, five already supported by experimental data, and argue the same framework can yield synapse-formation rules as expression coverage grows.
ocar.future_work: Improving single-cell profiling coverage should systematically expand falsifiable connection rules.

summaries.beginner: This work asks which gene pairs explain who touches whom in the worm’s nervous system. It predicts a small set of gap-junction protein partnerships, some already known from experiments, as a genetic sketch of the wiring.
summaries.intermediate: In 2020 work appearing as a PNAS-style study on this record, Kovács, Barabási, and Barabási link C. elegans adjacency to gene expression, including noise and spatial restrictions. They infer 19 innexin interactions that could govern gap-junction formation. Five of those interactions were already supported by experimental data.
summaries.advanced: 14 of 19 innexin interactions are predictions. Spatial constraints may absorb some residual error that is actually molecular. Chemical-synapse rules are prospective. Expression noise handling is necessary but can hide true weak rules.

plain_language_summary: This work asks which gene pairs explain who touches whom in the worm’s nervous system. It predicts a small set of gap-junction protein partnerships, some already known from experiments, as a genetic sketch of the wiring.

ocar.opportunity: Mechanisms that specify neuronal diversity are well known, but whether they also dictate circuit assembly is unclear. Mapping 160 fly larval interneurons from seven neuroblasts into a synapse-scale TEM volume can test that link.
ocar.challenge: Lineage, Notch hemilineage, and temporal identity must be related to neuropil targeting and connectivity, not only to cell type names.
ocar.action: Mark, Doe, Cardona and colleagues (eLife, 2019) mapped developmental origin of 160 interneurons from seven bilateral neuroblasts, identified them in a larval CNS TEM reconstruction, and analyzed targeting, connectome structure, and proximity versus specificity.
ocar.resolution: Lineages concurrently build sensory and motor neuropils via Notch-dependent sensory versus motor hemilineages. Hemilineage neurons share synaptic targeting, further refined by temporal identity, and hemilineage-temporal cohorts share connectivity. Proximity alone cannot explain that structure, so identity adds specificity and diversity-specifying mechanisms also govern circuit formation.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue these principles are broadly applicable throughout the nervous system.

summaries.beginner: How a brain cell is born—its family, its birth time, a yes/no developmental switch—might also decide who it wires to. In the fly maggot, cells from the same birth program really did share targets, more than sitting nearby would explain.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2019), Mark, Lai, Zarin, Cardona, Truman, Doe and colleagues linked neurogenesis to circuits for 160 Drosophila larval interneurons from seven bilateral neuroblasts identified in a synapse-scale TEM CNS reconstruction. Notch-dependent hemilineages concurrently build sensory and motor neuropils; hemilineage plus temporal identity predict targeting and shared connectivity. Proximity cannot explain the connectome structure, implicating identity in specificity.
summaries.advanced: The mapped set is 160 interneurons from seven neuroblast pairs, not the whole CNS. ‘Broadly applicable’ is an extrapolation. Notch hemilineage as sensory vs motor is the reported organizing split here; other lineages might differ. TEM identification depends on morphological matching into one volume.

plain_language_summary: How a brain cell is born—its family, its birth time, a yes/no developmental switch—might also decide who it wires to. In the fly maggot, cells from the same birth program really did share targets, more than sitting nearby would explain.

ocar.opportunity: FIB-SEM gives isotropic volumes ideal for ultrastructure and automated tracing but is limited in field of view and incompatible with ultrafast multibeam SEMs. Thick-section methods are multibeam-compatible but weak in z.
ocar.challenge: Bridging wide-area milling with <10 nm isotropic sampling, then stitching, is needed to keep segmentation-friendly z-resolution at larger scale.
ocar.action: Hayworth, Hess and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2019) demonstrated GCIB-SEM: gas-cluster ion-beam milling of thick sections, acquiring <10 nm isotropic stacks of each, then stitching across the sectioned volume, including work relevant to MICrONS-scale mouse tissue.
ocar.resolution: The method yields <10 nm isotropic datasets per thick section that can be stitched. Incorporating GCIB-SEM into single- and multibeam workflows is described as straightforward and as improving z-resolution by a factor of 3 or more while increasing reliability.
ocar.future_work: The pitch is integration with multibeam SEM for cubic-millimeter-scale connectomics at 10 nm isotropic.

summaries.beginner: One gold-standard 3D electron-microscope method is too small and slow for huge brains; cutting thick slices is faster but blurrier in depth. This work mills those thick slices with a wide ion beam so each slice can be imaged sharply in all three directions and then stacked.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2019), Hayworth, Hess and colleagues introduce GCIB-SEM: top-down wide-area gas-cluster ion milling of thick sections to collect sub-10 nm isotropic volumes. Those blocks are then stitched across the full sectioned sample. Aimed at combining FIB-SEM-like z-resolution with multibeam SEM fields of view, they estimate a z-resolution gain of threefold or more and greater reliability than classic thin-section methods.
summaries.advanced: ‘Straightforward’ integration is an authors’ claim. Stitching thick-section isotropic blocks can still accumulate alignment error at cube-millimeter scale. <10 nm is a target/demonstration class, not a full mm³ already acquired in the abstract. Comparison with FIB-SEM FOV limits is the motivation, not a bake-off table here.

plain_language_summary: One gold-standard 3D electron-microscope method is too small and slow for huge brains; cutting thick slices is faster but blurrier in depth. This work mills those thick slices with a wide ion beam so each slice can be imaged sharply in all three directions and then stacked.

ocar.opportunity: Community detection finds densely linked neural groups, but communities may hide smaller local integrator units such as interneuron sets whose connections stay inside the unit.
ocar.challenge: Standard algorithms stop at communities and miss those hidden local features; sensitivity to algorithm choice and network parameters is unknown.
ocar.action: Shi, Levina, and Noori (Physical Review E, 2019) combined Louvain communities with participation coefficients to split local neurons from global hubs, tested the scheme on synthetic networks, and applied it to weighted and binary C. elegans connectomes.
ocar.resolution: Detected local integrator units were distinctly localized in the worm body and defined functional groups. The authors offer this as observer-independent parcellation for architectonics and functional-connectivity analysis.
ocar.future_work: They suggest use on other species’ whole-brain graphs and on functional networks.

summaries.beginner: Network clustering often stops at large neighborhoods of cells. This method looks inside those neighborhoods for smaller pockets whose members mostly talk only to each other, and in the worm those pockets sat in sensible body locations and functional groups.
summaries.intermediate: In Physical Review E (2019), Shi, Levina, and Noori refine neuronal parcellation by finding local integrator units inside Louvain communities. Participation coefficients separate local cells from hubs, and simulations probe sensitivity to algorithm choice and network parameters. On weighted and binary C. elegans connectomes, the units were spatially localized and matched functional groups.
summaries.advanced: LU definition (all connections internal) is strict and may fragment real circuits with a few outgoing synapses. Dependence on Louvain plus participation coefficient is tested in simulation but remains a modeling choice. Functional-group agreement is anatomical interpretation.

plain_language_summary: Network clustering often stops at large neighborhoods of cells. This method looks inside those neighborhoods for smaller pockets whose members mostly talk only to each other, and in the worm those pockets sat in sensible body locations and functional groups.

ocar.opportunity: FlyCircuit offers morphology for a large fraction of the Drosophila brain, enabling a single-cell-level whole-brain spiking model if polarity, synapses, and physiology parameters can be estimated.
ocar.challenge: Image databases are not automatically simulation-ready: polarity, pairwise connections, and dynamics parameters must be inferred.
ocar.action: Huang, Chiang, Lo and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2018) built Flysim to assign arbor polarity, predict connections, translate morphology to physiology, reconstruct a 20,089-neuron, 1,044,020-synapse brain-wide network, simulate resting state, and compare with a shuffled-connection null.
ocar.resolution: The reconstructed brain stabilized with synaptic short-term depression, whereas the randomized network showed seizure-like firing under the same treatment. The reconstructed brain was structurally and dynamically more diverse, with both Poisson-like and patterned firing.
ocar.future_work: Even at this early stage, the model is offered to study balance, criticality, long-term stability, and plasticity at single-cell scale.

summaries.beginner: Researchers turned a large catalog of fruit-fly neuron shapes into a computer brain with about twenty thousand cells. The realistically wired version settled into mixed quiet and patterned activity, while a randomly rewired copy seized under the same rules.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2018), Huang et al. present Flysim, converting FlyCircuit morphologies into a Drosophila whole-brain spiking network: polarity identification, predicted connections, morphology-to-physiology mapping, then 20,089 neurons and 1,044,020 synapses. Resting-state simulations with short-term depression were stable for the reconstructed wiring but seizure-like after connection shuffling. The biological graph was more diverse, mixing Poisson-like and patterned firing.
summaries.advanced: Connections are predicted, not EM-verified. 20,089 neurons are a large but incomplete fly brain. Stability versus shuffle is under a specific STD treatment. Polarity inference errors would systematically bias excitation/inhibition balance. ‘Seizure-like’ is a dynamical description, not epilepsy biology.

plain_language_summary: Researchers turned a large catalog of fruit-fly neuron shapes into a computer brain with about twenty thousand cells. The realistically wired version settled into mixed quiet and patterned activity, while a randomly rewired copy seized under the same rules.

ocar.opportunity: Ciliary and rhabdomeric photoreceptors represent two evolutionary photoreceptor lines that coexist in some animals. Platynereis larvae offer a connectome-scale chance to see how the two systems interact during swimming.
ocar.challenge: How the two photoreceptor types are synaptically integrated, and how their behaviors combine, was unknown.
ocar.action: Verasztó, Jékely and colleagues (bioRxiv / eLife record, 2018) mapped synaptic paths between ciliary and rhabdomeric photoreceptors in the Platynereis larva, tested UV-driven swimming including in ciliary-opsin knockouts, and related vertical swimming to the blue/UV ratio.
ocar.resolution: Ciliary photoreceptors are presynaptic to the rhabdomeric circuit. They are UV-sensitive and mediate downward swimming to non-directional UV, absent in ciliary-opsin knockouts. UV avoidance antagonizes rhabdomeric-eye positive phototaxis, so vertical direction tracks the blue/UV ratio, which increases with depth—a spectral depth gauge.
ocar.future_work: The integration has implications for eye and photoreceptor evolution that invite comparison in other planktonic larvae.

summaries.beginner: A marine worm larva has two kinds of light sensors. Wiring and behavior experiments show the UV-sensitive kind sits upstream of the other and makes the larva swim down in UV, while the ratio of blue to UV light may tell it how deep it is.
summaries.intermediate: In 2018 work (eLife DOI on the record), Verasztó et al. used Platynereis connectomics to show ciliary photoreceptors synapse onto the rhabdomeric circuit. Ciliary cells are UV-sensitive and drive downward swimming to non-directional UV, lost in ciliary-opsin knockouts. This UV avoidance opposes rhabdomeric positive phototaxis, so vertical swimming follows the blue/UV ratio, a candidate depth gauge during planktonic migration.
summaries.advanced: Depth-gauge interpretation uses that blue/UV increases with depth as an optical fact plus the behavioral ratio rule; in situ vertical distributions are not in the abstract. Knockouts specifically support the UV-downward limb. Hierarchical antagonism is behavioral as well as synaptic.

plain_language_summary: A marine worm larva has two kinds of light sensors. Wiring and behavior experiments show the UV-sensitive kind sits upstream of the other and makes the larva swim down in UV, while the ratio of blue to UV light may tell it how deep it is.

ocar.opportunity: Most brain networks are directed at the synapse, but human imaging connectomes are undirected. Directed connectomes from cat, mouse, C. elegans, and macaque can quantify what is lost when arrows are dropped.
ocar.challenge: It is unknown how undirected surrogates distort degree, betweenness, clustering, path length, efficiency, participation, small-worldness, and hub identity.
ocar.action: Kale, Zalesky, and Gollo (Network Neuroscience, 2018) converted six directed connectomes to undirected ones by removing unidirectional edges, adding reciprocal edges, or mixing equal numbers of deletions and additions, then compared graph measures.
ocar.resolution: Core versus peripheral assignment stayed reasonably accurate, but hubs changed considerably. Adding false-positive reciprocal connections generally hurt measures more than deleting the same number of directed edges (false negatives). Directionality therefore shapes topology; undirected connectomes have important limits.
ocar.future_work: The false-positive versus false-negative asymmetry warns against filling in reciprocal edges when direction is unknown.

summaries.beginner: Human brain maps usually ignore which way a connection points, even though real synapses have a direction. Comparing animal maps with and without those arrows shows that the biggest hubs change, and that guessing missing reverse connections can distort the picture more than dropping one-way links.
summaries.intermediate: In Network Neuroscience (2018), Kale, Zalesky, and Gollo asked how ignoring direction distorts graph metrics, using six directed connectomes (cat, mouse, C. elegans, three macaque parcellations). Undirected versions were made by removing unidirectional edges, adding reciprocals, or mixing both. Core/periphery held up better than hub identity; adding false reciprocal edges typically caused larger errors than removing equally many directed edges.
summaries.advanced: Human MRI connectomes are not among the six; inference to humans is by analogy. Results depend on the three undirecting recipes. ‘Hubs differ considerably’ is the key caveat for anyone naming hubs on undirected graphs. Species and parcellation differences are grouped in the overall conclusion.

plain_language_summary: Human brain maps usually ignore which way a connection points, even though real synapses have a direction. Comparing animal maps with and without those arrows shows that the biggest hubs change, and that guessing missing reverse connections can distort the picture more than dropping one-way links.

ocar.opportunity: Connectome graphs capture fast synaptic transmission, but neurons also neuromodulate, changing properties rather than simply exciting or inhibiting. Extra chemical layers reconfigure the wiring diagram in use.
ocar.challenge: Network science on static synapses misses those adaptive extra-layers of interaction.
ocar.action: Hernández and Amigó (European Physical Journal Special Topics, 2018) propose multilayer adaptive networks as the right framework for neuronal processing and analyze a simplified model of interacting synaptic and neurochemical layers.
ocar.resolution: The simplified model is reported to show emergence of interesting computational capabilities from extra-layer interactions that condition and reconfigure the connectome.
ocar.future_work: The proposal is a modeling program: build connectome analyses that include neuromodulatory layers, not only the fast graph.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram of fast connections is not the whole conversation among brain cells; slower chemical signals retune those connections. This theory paper argues we should model brains as several interacting layers and shows a simple version that already computes in interesting ways.
summaries.intermediate: In European Physical Journal Special Topics (2018), Hernández and Amigó argue that connectome graph theory addresses fast neurotransmission but not neuromodulation. Neuromodulation reconfigures neuronal and synaptic properties rather than simply exciting or inhibiting. They propose multilayer adaptive networks as the framework and analyze a simplified model in which synaptic and neurochemical layers interact, reporting emergent computational capabilities.
summaries.advanced: No empirical connectome is fitted in the abstract. ‘Interesting computational capabilities’ is qualitative. The gap they identify is real, but the simplified model’s relation to any specific animal is unspecified here.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram of fast connections is not the whole conversation among brain cells; slower chemical signals retune those connections. This theory paper argues we should model brains as several interacting layers and shows a simple version that already computes in interesting ways.

ocar.opportunity: Industry-grade software practices have revived integrative, large-scale biological simulation. C. elegans, with cellular resolution and a known connectome, is a natural target for an open whole-animal model.
ocar.challenge: Combining diverse process-specific models into a coherent organism simulator requires organization, open science, and shared platforms.
ocar.action: Sarma, Larson and colleagues (Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 2018) overview the OpenWorm Foundation’s history, philosophy, sub-projects, management practices, achievements, and directions toward integrative C. elegans simulation.
ocar.resolution: OpenWorm is presented as an independent effort to simulate the worm so that behavior can be related to fundamental biology, as part of a discussion meeting on connectome-to-behaviour modeling at cellular resolution.
ocar.future_work: The perspective points to continued integration of sub-projects as the path to a usable whole-worm tool.

summaries.beginner: OpenWorm is an open project that tries to simulate the tiny worm C. elegans as a whole, from cells up to behavior. This article explains how the effort is organized and what it has achieved so far.
summaries.intermediate: In Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2018), Sarma, Larson and the OpenWorm community review an integrative C. elegans simulation program. The perspective covers history, philosophy, constituent sub-projects, and open-science management. It appears in a meeting issue on connectome-to-behaviour modeling at cellular resolution and sketches current achievements and future directions.
summaries.advanced: This is an organizational perspective, not a completed whole-animal simulation result. Success metrics for ‘integrative simulation’ remain distributed across sub-projects. Readers should treat it as a roadmap plus status, not a validation of worm-scale dynamics.
